Yellowing leaves this month are usually caused by the #1 seasonal mistake houseplant parents make. Here’s how to save your plant's life before it’s too late.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If your houseplant leaves are turning yellow this November, your plant is sending urgent distress signals that you really need to heed. As days shorten and sunlight becomes less intense in fall, most houseplants use far less moisture as their growth dramatically slows. Continuing your summer watering routine during this shift creates waterlogged soil, quickly leading to root rot – and an avoidable trip to the compost bin. Catch that first yellow leaf early, however, and you can quickly reverse the damage to keep your houseplant happy and healthy.

Failing to adjust a watering routine in line with houseplants’ seasonal needs is the most common mistake we plant parents make, and unfortunately the root rot that results can be fatal. It takes a few weeks of waterlogged soil and rotting roots before the damage manifests with yellowing leaves, which is why this symptom usually shows up in November – and why once you spot a yellowing leaf you need to take swift action.

So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your houseplant with a yellowing leaf, and save it from an untimely death with a simple fix.

Take a closer look at the yellow houseplant leaf to see what tone, shape, position and extent of the discoloration is. Different plants show this early symptom of root rot in various ways: a Monstera will likely get a yellow halo on one of its monster-sized leaves while a ZZ plant leaf will turn bright yellow from top to bottom overnight. Peperomia foliage typically fades to a pale yellow while a snake plant leaf takes on a translucent yellow tone at the base. Matching up the symptoms to the plant species is a surefire way to tell if overwatering is the cause.

Match your houseplant to the symptoms and you have your diagnosis.

Large, thin-leafed tropical plants like monstera, calathea, anthurium and clumping philodendron typically show a bright yellow halo around a dark spot from overwatering. This happens because as roots begin to rot in soggy soil, fungal or bacterial pathogens in the potting mix travel up the plant and into the leaf tissue. Dead leaf cells show up as a black or brown area, and the bright ring of yellow around it is where the plant is attempting to stop the infection spreading.

ZZ plants (Zamioculcas zamiifolia), caladiums, and elephant ears (Alocasia and Colocasia) grow from potato-like rhizomes or tubers that store lots of water, so it can take these plants a little longer to show signs of overwatering. When they do, it's dramatic though! If these houseplants receive more water than they can process and rot sets in, nutrients are suddenly cut to a whole stem. The entire stalk and its foliage will quickly drain of color to turn a solid strong yellow, top to bottom.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Prayer plants (Maranta), peperomia, Chinese money plants (Pilea peperomioides), African violets (Saintpaulia), nerve plants (Fittonia) and Boston and maidenhair ferns all have a shallow network of very fine, fragile roots. Suffocating in overwatered soil, these thin roots quickly disintegrate and the leaves lose their lustre then become limp and fade through pale green to a matte yellow. Don’t expect these leaves to be mushy from all that water: because the root damage cuts the water supply off, leaves will become dry and brittle, snapping off immediately when touched or simply dropping from the plant.

Jade plants (Crassula ovata), snake plants, Christmas or Thanksgiving cacti (Schlumbergera), echeverias and aloe vera all store water in their stems or leaves, and excess moisture causes them to turn a translucent, sickly yellow at the base. The area will also feel mushy and this may happen where stems or leaves meet the soil, in which case stems may topple over, but also where leaves attach to stems or leaf segments join together.

Vining plants like pothos (Epipremnum aureum), English ivy (Hedera helix), wax plants (Hoya) and heartleaf philodendron (Philodendron hederaceum) typically show overwatering symptoms on their oldest leaves near the base first. Unable to draw as many nutrients through suffocating roots, the plant strips nutrients from its older, less productive leaves to feed the fresh growth at its tips in the hope of finding a more suitable environment. Stripped of chlorophyll, the base foliage turns an even, uniform yellow while the newer growth at the stem tip remains green.

Overwatered houseplants with long, narrow leaves like spider plants (Chlorophytum comosum) and ponytail palms (Beaucarnea recurvata) typically develop brown foliage tips with a yellow area separating them from the healthy green tissue. This happens because the leaf tips are at the very end of the plant's plumbing system so, when roots are damaged and can't take up water effectively, are the first to run out of moisture. The yellow color below the dead brown leaf tissue is the plant trying to salvage what nutrients it can. The leaves may lose their upright arch and start to droop, too.

If you spot yellowing houseplant leaves, immediately stop watering and let the soil dry out. Slide the pot off and if you see white roots, you’ve caught the problem in time. Pop the plant back into its pot and only water when the top inch of potting mix feels dry. A moisture meter like this from Amazon takes out the guesswork and helps you adjust your routine to the plant's fluctuating needs going forwards, and water houseplants properly.

If there’s a foul, stagnant smell, however faint, and roots look dark, root rot has set in and you’ll need to take action to save your plant. Remove as much soil as possible and use sharp scissors or pruners or to snip off all roots that look dark or feel mushy or slimy. Rinse the roots and wash the pot, then repot your houseplant.

It's vital the pot has a drainage hole so excess moisture can escape (and a saucer to save your surfaces). If you adore a decorative hole-less pot, use it as a cachepot with a holed plastic pot inside. For succulent plants that store water in their leaves or stems, fill your pot with a fast-draining potting mix like Back to the Roots Organic Succulents & Cacti Mix, available from The Home Depot. For everything else, use an indoor potting mix with coconut coir and perlite that evens out moisture levels while allowing good drainage like Miracle-Gro Indoor Potting Mix For All Plants, available from Walmart.

Upgrade your irrigation with a watering can that has a long, gooseneck spout like this indoor can from Walmart for more precise, controlled water delivery.

End rot is a common challenge for winter squash in fall but identify the cause and it's simple to rescue the remaining crop.

A lost leaf or two doesn’t spell disaster for a Christmas cactus in fall but you can't afford to ignore this distress signal.

Chafer grubs have devastated drought-stressed lawns this year but are easily treated if catch this crucial fall window.

Work out what your peace lily needs to recover if spathes develop brown patches or look dry and crispy around the edges.

Tulip fire can make your eagerly anticipated spring bulbs look distorted and spotty. But these quick bulb planting checks can help you to prevent calamity later

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Planting some tulips is one of the most enjoyable ways to pass some time this month. It offers the promise of vivid, saturated color to punctuate the winter months. Too often, however, the anticipation can turn to heartbreak, as early leaves emerge stunted, twisted, and scarred with spots. This is classic tulip fire: an aggressive fungal blight that leaves tulips looking as though they were scorched by an open flame.

The frustrating reality of tulip fire is that while symptoms appear in spring, the infection usually begins months earlier during tulip planting. The pathogen enters unnoticed on dry bulb scales, or lies dormant in beds where infected tulips grew before. Once established, no post-planting drench or spray can save infected stems. Your best defense is prevention before your tulip bulbs go in the ground. A few careful checks at planting time give next year's tulips a much better shot. Just a few proactive measures this fall will ensure that your tulips emerge clean, robust, and full of vibrant blooms. Here’s how to address the perils of tulip fire before it ever has a chance to cause problems – so you can look forward to spring with confidence.

Tulip fire is a common tulip disease caused by the fungal pathogen Botrytis tulipae. While closely related to common gray mold (B. cinerea), which attacks soft fruits and perennials, B. tulipae is host-specific and targets tulips almost exclusively. This host specificity is an advantage for gardeners. If you deny the fungus its preferred host for 3-4 seasons, resting populations in the soil gradually starve and decline.

Recognizing early symptoms is key to containment. In early spring, infected bulbs send up stunted, crumpled shoots known as fireheads. These sickly stems become blanketed in fuzzy gray fungal spores that blow or splash onto neighboring plants during cool, rainy weather. Tiny, water-soaked flecks quickly spread across foliage, coalescing into scorched brown blotches, while flower buds rot before opening. Wet spring conditions across USDA hardiness zones 3-8 accelerate spore dispersal, and can turn an isolated infection into an outbreak within a week.

Most cultivated tulip hybrids are at risk in damp, overcrowded conditions. However, species tulips with lower profiles (like Tulipa clusiana or T. tarda) and sturdy Darwin hybrid varieties demonstrate better resilience than dense, double-flowered late types. If you’re still deciding which bulbs to get, try bold Red Darwin Hybrid Tulip Bulbs from Amazon for weather resistant stems, and dreamily elegant Salmon Impression Darwin Hybrid Tulip Bulbs from Plant Addicts for natural vigor. Here's how to prevent your tulips turning into fireheads. Grab your bulbs and get ready!

Preventing tulip fire adds only a few minutes to your fall planting routine, but the benefits are immeasurable. Proactive defense focuses on basic cultural care: thoughtful checks, site and timing prep, and ample airflow. The following simple checks take just a little extra preparation, providing peace of mind and protecting your spring displays long before the first green shoots pierce the soil…

Before planting your bulbs, empty your bulb bags onto an outdoor potting bench or table, and inspect each one individually. A healthy, viable tulip bulb should feel solid, firm, and dense, with an intact papery outer tunic. Gently press the base plate and tip with your thumb. Any that give under your thumb, show mold, feel spongy, or have sunken yellow-brown patches should go in the trash.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Next, peel back a section of the papery tunic. Look carefully for sclerotia: tiny, hard, black or dark-brown resting bodies that resemble crushed pepper or poppy seeds. To help get a better look up close, the Jarlink 30X 60X Illuminated Jewelers Loupe, available from Amazon is equipped with bright LED illumination to check for those black sclerotia specks, as well as hidden scale lesions. These small sclerotia carry the tulip fire fungus between seasons. If you detect black specks or lesions, bag the bulb and throw it in the trash. Never toss diseased stock into home compost piles.

Resist the urge to plant your tulips while the ground is still warm. Botrytis tulipae fungal spores and resting sclerotia thrive in mild, damp soil conditions between 50°F and 65°F (10-18°C). Planting prematurely exposes bulbs to active soil-borne pathogens before the bulbs can establish robust roots. Delay your tulip planting until mid-to-late November or early December across most regions, after several hard overnight frosts have chilled the ground.

Soil temperatures should consistently measure below 50°F (10°C) at 6 inches (15cm). Cold soil suppresses fungal activity and forces dormant spores into inactivity. Planting after the first hard frosts is one of the most effective defenses against tulip fire. Even if an early frost hardens the surface, the soil beneath remains workable. Using a long-handled bulb planter like the Jardineer Bulb Transplanter from The Home Depot works well even in frost-encrusted fall soils.

Soil hygiene and thoughtful rotation are critical defenses against tulip fire. If your border suffered from tulip fire last spring, millions of sclerotia will have been shed into the earth as the leaves and flower petals decomposed. These resting bodies can survive in loam for 3-5 years, waiting to infect any new tulips that push up through the contaminated soil, and start the cycle all over again. Give that bed at least 3 years without tulips, and plant new bulbs somewhere that's never had the disease. Fill affected borders with non-host species that tulip fire cannot infect, such as daffodils (narcissus), alliums, grape hyacinths (muscari), or crocuses.

If bed space is tight, containers are an easy workaround. Transition your tulips into patio containers. However, always dump out old potting soil, sanitize containers with a dilute vinegar or mild bleach wash, and plant in fresh, sterile soilless potting mix enriched with perlite. A lovely blend is Espoma Organic Potting Mix, available from Walmart, which is free of garden pathogens, and gives a low-release nutrient boost.

A bulb that sits in soggy ground all winter is in trouble, whether tulip fire shows up or not. Good drainage is critical. Tulip bulbs thrive in moisture, but can rot quickly in stagnant water. Planting in heavy, compacted clay or low-lying depressions also creates damp conditions where fungal spores multiply rapidly. Check your planting site a day or so after a soaking rain. Water that is still standing there, or dirt that balls up and sticks to your boots, means the spot would drain too slowly for tulips.

Select a planting site situated on high ground or a gentle slope. If you garden on heavy clay, avoid digging individual narrow holes. Instead, excavate the whole planting area 8-10 inches (20-30cm) deep. Blend some horticultural grit or coarse sand into the soil to help with drainage. Alternatively, for persistently soggy gardens, skip the fight and grow your tulips in containers or raised beds. You can get small bags of best-selling Miracle-Gro Perlite from The Home Depot for just a few dollars, and sprinkle a few handfuls into the planting site (or use it in your containers!).

Crowded planting designs may look lush in magazine spreads, but tightly packed bulbs create stagnant, humid conditions. After a few years, offsets and daughter bulbs fill in a bit more each season, and after a while the leaves will crowd each other. If tulips are jammed together, leaves that touch will stay wet longer after rain or a heavy dew, and spores won't have far to go to get from one plant to the next.

Give your tulips room to breathe by spacing bulbs 4-6 inches (10-15cm) apart in all directions. Make sure the planting site is not jammed against a fence or the side of the house. Choose open, sunny sites with steady airflow. Use jute twine like Vivifying Natural Jute from Amazon looped around some wooden stakes to help mark your plantings. Also, if you are naturalizing tulips in mixed borders, lift and divide dense perennial clumps every few years before planting your bulbs.

Old tulip leaves don't just vanish when they're left on the soil. On plants that were sick, fresh sclerotia form on the dying tissue and drop into the bed, and they can stay there until tulips come up through that ground again. Infected leaves, decaying stem bases, and dropped flower petals all produce fresh sclerotia as they wither. Left untouched, it decomposes into the topsoil, recharging the fungal spore bank.

Before planting new bulbs, do a fall cleanup. Rake through your beds and clear out old leaves, spent stems, and decayed organic matter. Pull back mulch to inspect the soil, discarding any dried plant remnants and flower parts from the previous growing season. Make sure you bag these remnants instead of composting them. You can buy best-selling Fabulas Yard Waste Bags from Walmart in triple packs.

In spring, you need to stay proactive. Deadhead any spent flowers off suspect plants before their petals drop onto lower foliage, and clear out leaves and stems from anything that shows symptoms. Dig up any twisted firehead shoots, including the bulbs and adjacent soil. Do this the moment symptoms appear to keep airborne spores from spreading. Cleanup won't necessarily promise a clean bed, but it ensures there's a lot less fungus left behind to start the next round.

Once tulip fire takes hold in an established bed, it is one of the most persistent and frustrating bulb diseases to eradicate. So this fall care routine is massively beneficial in helping to break the fungal life cycle before it can cause damage. Take the right steps now when planting, and then you just have to wait for those first green shoots and a vibrant, spotless tulip display in spring.

#8006. How to Test Your Home’s Water Quality

Published Nov 3, 2026 12:05 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

We use water every day for drinking, cooking, cleaning, and bathing, but how often do we stop to think about what’s actually in it? Water that looks clean can contain potentially harmful contaminants, including lead, bacteria, and chemicals. The good news is, learning how to test water quality at home is pretty straightforward, whether you’re using an inexpensive DIY test kit, or you mail a sample to a certified laboratory. We’ll walk you through the testing process, explain what your results mean, and help you figure out what to do if you find a problem.

Even if your water looks clean doesn’t always mean it’s safe to drink. Contaminants and certain bacteria can be in there without changing the water’s appearance, taste, or smell. Testing your water helps identify potential health risks and gives you a clearer picture of what’s coming out of your faucets.

“A common misconception is that water is safe if it looks, smells and tastes fine,” says Dr. Eric Roy, Chief of Science at Culligan International. “But the reality is that contaminants such as lead, arsenic, and ‘forever chemicals’ (PFAS) cannot be detected by our senses.”

Water testing can also reveal less serious issues, such as high mineral content. Hard water, which contains elevated levels of calcium and magnesium, can cause scale buildup in pipes and appliances, leave spots on dishes, and make soap less effective. Testing can also help you get to the bottom of unpleasant tastes, unusual odors, or discoloration.

Knowing what’s in your water helps you decide whether you need a filtration system, a water softener, or another treatment method. And even if your water is perfectly safe to drink, you might still want to improve its taste or overall quality.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Testing your water quality is a simple process that takes just a few minutes of hands-on work, depending on the type of test you choose. At-home water test kits give you quick results for common water-quality indicators, while mail-in laboratory tests offer more detailed information about potentially harmful contaminants.

Before getting started, read the instructions included with your test kit carefully. Different tests have different sampling requirements, and even small mistakes, such as touching the inside of a collection bottle or flushing the faucet when you shouldn’t, can affect the accuracy of your results.

The best testing method depends on what you’re looking for. Inexpensive, at-home test kits typically use strips or color-changing solutions to check for pH, chlorine, and hardness. They’re useful for identifying common water-quality issues, but generally lack the precision to detect harmful contaminants at very low concentrations.

For health-related concerns, such as lead, arsenic, bacteria, or PFAS, choose a mail-in kit analyzed by a certified laboratory. As Dr. Jess Goddard, chief science officer at SimpleLab Inc. explains, “If you’re making a health decision or about to spend money on treatment, you definitely want lab results behind it.”

Safe Home’s mail-in water test kit checks 200 qparameters, including 7 inorganics, 31 metals, and 20 pesticides and herbicides. Read the review.

Before collecting your water sample, wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water and clear the area around the faucet. Wipe away any visible dirt or debris, and remove the faucet aerator if your testing instructions require it. Some tests, particularly those for bacteria, may also require disinfecting the faucet opening before sampling.

Be careful not to introduce contaminants during preparation. Avoid touching the inside of collection bottles or their caps, and wear disposable gloves if recommended by your test kit. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, as preparation requirements can vary depending on the contaminants being tested.

For many water tests, you’ll need to run cold water through the faucet for a couple of minutes before collecting your sample. This flushes out stagnant water that’s been sitting in your plumbing, helping you collect a sample representative of your incoming water supply. However, always check your kit’s instructions first, as some tests require a different approach.

“For example, some lead-testing protocols require collecting the first water from a cold tap after several hours without use,” explains Rich Razgaitis, co-founder and CEO of FloWater. “If you flush the pipes beforehand, you may wash away the very evidence you’re looking for.”

Once the faucet is prepared, collect your sample according to your test kit’s instructions. The process differs slightly depending on your testing method:

Keep your fingers away from bottle openings and inside surfaces to prevent contamination. Seal samples immediately and follow any storage or shipping instructions.

Now it’s time to test your sample. The process will depend on whether you’re using an at-home kit or sending your water to a laboratory.

Note: At-home kits aren’t always dip strips. Some use reagents, test vials, or incubation procedures for bacteria. Always follow the instructions for the specific kit you have.

Once you’ve tested your water, the next step is figuring out what the results mean. Most at-home testing kits use color-coded charts to indicate the concentration of different substances in your water, while laboratory reports provide more precise measurements, often in parts per million (ppm), parts per billion (ppb), or milligrams per liter (mg/L).

Compare your results with the reference ranges provided by the kit or laboratory, paying particular attention to any contaminants that exceed health-based guidelines. Keep in mind that detecting a substance doesn’t automatically mean your water is unsafe.

“When interpreting results, a common mistake is assuming that a detection automatically means you have a health risk,” explains Goddard. “You need to put the result in context, first, and compare the detected concentration to a health guideline to determine if there’s a problem.”

Here’s what some common water-quality findings mean and how to address them.

Water hardness measures the concentration of dissolved minerals, primarily calcium and magnesium. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, water containing 121 to 180 ppm of hardness (measured as calcium carbonate) is considered hard, while anything above 180 ppm is very hard.

Hard water is generally safe to drink, but it can cause mineral buildup in pipes, faucets, and appliances. If your results indicate hard or very hard water and you’re experiencing these problems, consider installing a water softener. These systems reduce calcium and magnesium levels to help prevent scale buildup.

iSpring’s water softener is an electronic magnetic softener that treats mineral buildup but doesn’t remove heavy metals from water. Read the review.

Lead can enter drinking water through old pipes, solder, and plumbing fixtures, particularly in older homes. There is no known safe level of lead exposure, so any detected lead deserves attention, especially in households with children.

If a lab test detects lead, use a verified safe drinking-water source while investigating the problem. Contact your water utility or local health department for guidance, and consider having your plumbing inspected. A water filter independently certified for lead reduction can help reduce exposure, but replacing lead-containing plumbing may be necessary to address the source.

Finding E. coli in drinking water is a serious concern because it indicates fecal contamination. If your test detects E. coli, stop drinking the untreated water and contact your local health department or water utility.

For private wells, a professional may recommend inspecting and disinfecting the well, followed by additional testing to confirm the water is safe. UV treatment or other disinfection systems may also be appropriate for certain ongoing bacterial problems.

Boiling water can kill many disease-causing microorganisms, but it won’t remove chemical contaminants such as lead or nitrates. Follow the specific guidance provided by your health department rather than assuming boiling will solve every water-quality problem.

Nitrates can enter groundwater through fertilizers, septic systems, and agricultural runoff. Elevated levels are particularly dangerous for infants because they can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen.

The EPA’s drinking-water limit for nitrate is 10 mg/L measured as nitrogen (NO3-N). If your results exceed this level, switch to a verified safe water source for drinking, cooking, and preparing baby formula, and consult your local health department.

A reverse osmosis system certified for nitrate reduction may be an appropriate long-term solution. Do not boil nitrate-contaminated water, as evaporation can increase the nitrate concentration.

Arsenic and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) can be present in drinking water without any noticeable change in taste, smell, or appearance. Both can pose health risks, depending on the substance and concentration.

If lab testing identifies levels above applicable health-based guidelines, use a verified safe drinking-water source while seeking advice from your health department or a qualified water-treatment professional.

Depending on the contaminant, an appropriately certified reverse osmosis or activated carbon filtration system may help. Check that the specific system has been tested and certified to reduce the substance identified in your results.

The Waterdrop G3P600 installs under the sink and has a digital display that monitors the presence of TDS in the water. Read the review.

Not every unusual result indicates a health risk. Elevated iron can cause reddish-brown staining, while chlorine may give treated municipal water an unpleasant taste or odor. High mineral concentrations can also affect how water tastes.

If testing confirms that the issue is aesthetic rather than a health concern, you may be able to address it with a relatively simple treatment system. Activated carbon filters can improve chlorine taste and odor, while specialized iron filters can help reduce staining caused by elevated iron levels.

“A filter that improves taste isn’t necessarily removing lead,” says Razgaitis. “A water softener addresses hardness, not every health concern. UV treatment targets microorganisms but doesn’t remove dissolved chemicals.”

Whatever your results show, choose a treatment system that is independently certified to address the specific contaminants in your water, rather than assuming any filter will do the job.

Testing your home’s water quality is a simple but important step toward making sure the water you use every day is safe. Whether you use an at-home testing kit or send a sample to a certified laboratory, following the proper collection instructions will help you get reliable results.

Remember: Not every unusual reading indicates a health risk, but potentially harmful contaminants should always be taken seriously. Once you understand what’s in your water, you can make informed decisions about whether filtration, water softening, or other treatment is necessary.

Yes, you can test your home’s water quality using an at-home testing kit. Most kits use test strips or chemical reagents to check for common water-quality indicators such as pH, chlorine, and hardness. However, DIY kits have limitations, particularly when detecting potentially harmful contaminants at very low concentrations. For more comprehensive testing, the EPA recommends using a state-certified drinking water laboratory.

Common signs of poor water quality include unusual tastes or odors, cloudy or discolored water, and staining around sinks and faucets. White, chalky residue on fixtures can also indicate hard water. However, these symptoms don’t necessarily mean your water is unsafe. According to the CDC, harmful germs and chemicals may be present without affecting how water looks, tastes, or smells.

At-home water tests are a convenient, inexpensive way to screen for basic water-quality issues, such as hardness, pH, and chlorine levels. However, laboratory testing is generally the better option if you’re concerned about contaminants such as lead, arsenic, PFAS, or bacteria. These tests require greater accuracy and sensitivity than most DIY kits can provide. For example, the CDC recommends using a state-certified laboratory to test private well water.

There’s no single list of five indicators that covers every drinking-water concern, but homeowners should pay particular attention to total coliform bacteria, nitrates, pH, total dissolved solids (TDS), and lead.

#8005. Kathy’s Fall Garden

Happy Monday, GPOD! Halloween may be behind us, but fall still has plenty to offer in Kathy’s Zone 6a garden. I love how she keeps the seasonal decorating simple and lets what’s already happening in the landscape do most of the work. A few pumpkins, a refreshed container, and plants still hanging onto their color are enough to make the whole front garden feel ready for November.

Keeping it sweet and simple this fall! It has been a beautiful fall in Michigan so far. Although I’ve been gardening for more than 40 years, this is my eighth year gardening at our current home in Macomb.

I love these Japanese forest grasses (Hakonechloa macra cvs., Zones 5–9).

I replaced this summer container display earlier than usual, and these plants have been hanging tough since the first week of September.

Just sweet! There has been a multitude of fancy pumpkins for sale this year, more than usual, and I think they are so pretty!

Boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), Fire Chief arborvitae (Thuja occidentalis ‘Congabe’, Zones 5–8), ‘Orange Rocket’ Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii ‘Orange Rocket’, Zones 4–9), and Little Lime® panicle hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata ‘Jane’, Zones 3–8) grow in front of our home.

Already, I’m looking forward to spring when I can plant this new garden arch! I’m thinking clematis (Clematis cvs., Zones 3–9).

Here is Belleza Dark Pink gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri ‘KLEAU04263’, Zones 6–9) and yellow ‘Lady Stratheden’ avens (Geum ‘Lady Stratheden’, Zones 5–9). They are hanging tough so far!

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Kathy! I really like the little bed by the driveway. The purple tones of the ajuga carpeting the ground against that bright orange mum and the pumpkins make for such an effortlessly beautiful fall display. And I’m with you on already thinking about spring—I’d love to see what you decide to grow over that new arch!

Why plant an invasive ornamental tree when you could have one that's just as beautiful but brings so much more to the garden?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Look, I'm calling it: the Bradford pear has had its moment. For years, its blooms have been everywhere, but now its the turn of an even prettier native tree to take its spot – and it definitely helps that it's a triple threat when it comes to blossoms, berries, and beautiful fall foliage!

I know, I know; it's a big claim, especially as so many people rate the Bradford pear for its frothy white flowers, not to mention the pretty show its leaves put on when fall arrives. Still, there's a less attractive side to Bradford pears – and I'm not just talking about the unpleasant stench its flowers put out.

That's right, folks! As well as being notoriously unpleasant-smelling, the Bradford pear's branches are prone to splitting, and these trees can contribute to the spread of invasive Callery pears, too. So, if you're thinking about planting a new ornamental tree, it might be time to consider a more wildlife-friendly alternative.

My suggested swap for the invasive Bradford pear? Why, the serviceberry, of course!

This beautiful native tree pretty much does it all; think plenty of springtime charm in the form of beautiful blossoms, followed by delicious berries, and wrapped up nicely with some gorgeous fall foliage. And unlike Bradford pear, it's a valuable addition to a garden that welcomes local wildlife.

Serviceberry, also known as juneberry or shadbush, belongs to the Amelanchier genus. Depending on the species and variety, it can grow as a large shrub or a small tree, making it a useful option for gardens where a full-sized shade tree would be too much.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

It is one of those plants that gives back much more than it takes, providing an early source of nectar and pollen for pollinators, sweet edible berries that work brilliantly in pies, jams and other homemade treats (although birds love them, too), and gorgeous fall foliage that promises to paint your yard in shades of yellow, orange and red before winter arrives.

All that from one relatively compact native tree? You'd better believe it!

One of the things I love most about serviceberry (as if all of the above weren't reason enough to be a fan!) is that most species grow well in full sun or partial shade, making it more accessible to people with all sorts of gardens. Just be sure to pop it in a spot with well-draining soil, as they won't appreciate sitting in waterlogged ground.

For many homeowners, this native tree is a no-brainer, because what do you mean it offers the spring flowers that made Bradford pear so popular, along with edible fruit, beautiful fall color and valuable food for wildlife? Tick, tick, tick, and tick!

While it won't necessarily grow as quickly or have the same uniform, upright shape as a Bradford pear, I think that's part of its appeal. And, with the world changing as quickly as it is, I think we can all agree that a garden tree should do more than look pretty for a few weeks each year.

A native beauty that gives back to local critters and puts out fruit that taste every bit as good as blueberries, then? Sign me up!

Peonies are pretty, we know, but peony-like tulips give you way more petals for far less effort, and you can plant the spring-flowering bulbs in November.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We all adore the richly-colored, ruffled petals of peonies but if you’ve only got one plant in your garden, the show’s over in little more than a week. Plant some peony-like tulip bulbs, however, and you can enjoy months of very similar-looking flowers from early April all through May and sometimes even into June. These double tulips couldn’t be easier to grow, and this month is the exact right time to plant the bulbs.

Most tulips have six petals but a natural genetic hiccup capitalized upon by plant breeders means that some cultivars can have up to 50 packed into a single bloom. They’re known as double tulips, and their petal-explosion flowers look remarkably similar to peony blooms. Typically hardy in zones 3-8, they’re some of the best tulip varieties to kickstart spring in your garden, and the most striking spring-flowering bulbs to plant in November.

The trick to enjoying months of flowers is to pick a pair of tulip varieties, one that opens early and one that blooms a little later. Early-flowering double tulips (officially known as peony-like tulips) begin blooming early in April. These tend to have shorter, sturdy 12-16 inch-high stems so stand up well to spring storms. Their tight layers of petals protect the flower core from cold weather, too, so each bloom can last for around 3 weeks – far longer than a standard tulip.

Late-flowering double tulips (known as peony-flowered tulips) bloom late April through May and are even more spectacular with huge flower heads on taller 16-24 inch-high stems. Because they're so top-heavy, these are more vulnerable to toppling in strong winds so in an exposed garden, give them a sheltered spot.

So, if you love peony flowers and you're wondering what to plant in November, look no further. Part of the Weekend Wins series, planting double tulips that look like peonies is one of those easy garden jobs that brings a big reward.

When shopping for double tulips, it's important that bulbs are big enough to fuel all those petals so early in the year, so always buy from a quality supplier. All our recommendations are for 10 bulbs.

‘Lorenzo’ gets spring off to a cheery start with long-lasting blooms in a luminous apricot-orange softly edged in creamy yellow, all through April.

With enormous blooms opening in late April and peaking through May, ‘Gudoshnik Double' has painterly petals streaked in yellow, orange and red.

A few double tulips are fragranced, and 'Avant Garde’ opens its buds in early April to release a sweet, floral perfume with beautifully fresh undertones.

In late April, ‘Pistache’ brings more creamy-white petals, this time splashed with wine red, and a wonderful scent of almonds and pistachios into May.

‘Foxy Foxtrot’ wakes up early in April, opening a lovely lemon yellow then gaining rich, warm tones of apricot, salmon-pink and honeyed gold.

In mid-to-late April, ‘Amazing Grace’ starts in a soft lavender pink with green accents, then shade-shifts into a deep rose tone that lasts deep into May.

In early April, ‘Royal Acres’ blooms open into bowls of intensely-colored, velvety magenta petals, often with a silvery sheen along the ruffled edges.

‘Dream Touch’ takes over the show from late April through May with enormous purple blooms, their striking petals prettily edged in white.

Though officially classified as a late tulip, ‘Mariage’ blooms in mid-April with deeply ruffled flowers in the prettiest pale rose-pink, and lasts into May.

‘Wild Romance’ adds creamy white petals with blushing pink picotee edges from late April through May, opening to reveal dramatic jet-black stamens.

‘Marshmallow’ opens in early April with a splash of bi-colored raspberry pink and ivory white petals, with a few green streaks for good measure.

Keeping the drama going, ‘Black Hero’, blooms from late April through May with ruffles of velvety deep-maroon petals that have a super sheen.

Growing spectacular double tulip flowers from fall-planted bulbs couldn’t be easier, and November is the exact right time to get them in the ground.

A real Christmas tree doesn't have to be disposable. Choose the right variety, and your festive centerpiece can have a whole new life outdoors.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there is one piece of decor that represents the holidays, it’s got to be a Christmas tree. Add an evergreen tree to your living room, toss on some tinsel, and, suddenly, it’s the holidays.

But Christmas trees seem more expensive every year, and it’s not fun to spend all that money on a one-use tree that you'll discard in January. This is the year to switch to a beautiful live Christmas tree that lasts for years. There are lots of miniature Christmas-type trees that can be grown in pots, spruced up for the holiday, then enjoyed in the garden for the rest of the year.

The key is to buy a living tree that is attractive and built for the long haul, not a single use. I’ve got you covered on that score with a short list of the best living Christmas tree options, from miniature traditional-looking spruces to unusual blue and golden conifers.

What’s the best small evergreen tree to grow in a pot for Christmas? Well, the answer will be different for each of us. There are plenty of attractive trees that make good live Christmas trees through December, then live happily in the garden the rest of the year. Pick your favorite, but make sure it’s suited to your USDA hardiness zone so it can thrive outdoors for years to come!

Dwarf Alberta spruce (Picea glauca 'Conica') makes wonderful live, potted Christmas trees. These trees offer a classic pyramidal Christmas tree shape and incredible longevity – to 50 years or more in the right conditions. Their compact, densely packed growth habit makes these trees look cute, and they grow very slowly – between 2 and 4 inches (2.5–5 cm) per year – and top out at just over 10 feet (3 m) tall and wide. The needles are fine-textured and soft to the touch, a rich blue-green. They are also aromatic when rubbed.

You can order a classic dwarf Alberta spruce online at Nature Hills, or for something a little different, the Rainbow's End cultivar, which produces a second flush of lemon-yellow growth in summer.

These little spruces are easy to care for, drought-tolerant, and cold-tolerant. They grow best in well-drained acidic soil and prefer full sun. Only water when the top 3 inches of soil are dry. Their preferred climate (USDA zones 2–8) has cold winters and cool summers.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A dwarf blue spruce (Picea pungens 'Globosa') can make a great compact, living Christmas tree. You can doll it up for the holidays indoors, then move this slow-growing evergreen conifer outdoors for the winter in USDA zones 2–8. It needs little maintenance and offers a tidy, manageable size and striking silver-blue foliage.

The signature blue needles make the dwarf spruce a unique holiday tree, and its strong, stiff branches hold up heavy ornaments without issue. The natural pyramidal form requires little shaping, and its needles rarely fall out. On the other hand, the needles are prickly and can hurt you when you are decorating if you aren’t careful. Plus, this spruce doesn’t offer the beloved evergreen aroma, but a distinct odor that isn’t universally loved.

Dwarf blue spruce trees require very little attention once established. When you are moving the tree outside, put it in a site with lots of direct sun. Add several inches of organic mulch to the soil. The ‘Globosa’ cultivar, available from Woodies Garden Goods, reaches 3 to 5 feet (1–1.5 m) tall and wide.

Korean fir (Abies koreana) is a compact, slow-growing, symmetrical evergreen tree. With its soft, rounded needles and dense growth habit, it is a popular choice for a live Christmas tree.

The needles are very ornamental, a dark green with a silvery underside, and offer a rich, fresh forest scent with notes of citrus. The cones are special too, a striking violet-purple and stand upright. This slow-growing fir creeps up a bit every year to finish at some 15-30 feet tall, with a conical form. A species tree will grow to 30 feet (10 m) tall, but a dwarf variety like Cis Dwarf Korean Fir, from Nature Hills, stops at 2 to 3 feet tall and wide. For something different, Ice Breaker Korean Fir is a dwarf variety that looks perpetually snow-covered.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, acidic soil. These trees thrive in USDA zones 5–7.

A dwarf Norway spruce (Picea abies) makes a charming, compact live Christmas tree that can be kept in a pot or, in zones 3–7, planted in the garden after the holidays. These small trees typically reach around 3 feet (1 m) tall and wide at maturity, depending on the cultivar. They make charming, sustainable live Christmas trees and can be moved outdoors after the festive season.

A dwarf Norway spruce tree offers a classic triangular shape, dark green needles, and graceful, drooping branchlets. This classic Christmas tree is popular for its dense, symmetrical shape and rich "Christmassy" scent that quickly fills up the room. Unfortunately, Norway spruce needles can dry out and drop fast in warm indoor temperatures, so keep it in as cool a spot as possible.

These trees are generally about 3 feet tall (90 cm) when sold as potted Christmas trees, and the ultimate height depends on the cultivar. They grow slowly, adding between 1 and 3 inches (5–10 cm) every year.

You can buy both ‘Pumila’ dwarf Norway spruce and ‘Pusch’ dwarf Norway spruce at Nature Hills. ‘Pumila’ has a dense, bushy shape that looks lovely decorated for Christmas, while ‘Pusch’ offers something a little different, producing tiny red cones in spring that add extra interest to the garden.

Japanese cedars (Cryptomeria japonica) make unique live Christmas trees with soft, fine foliage that is pleasant to touch. The appearance depends on the cultivar, but many compact cultivars offer a naturally dense, rounded shape. The foliage can take on bronze, copper, or bluish-green tones during winter.

For a real statement tree, Black Dragon Japanese cedar, available from Plant Addicts, has a mature height of 8–10 feet (2.5–3 m), or for a smaller tree, the Tansu Dwarf Japanese cedar, from Nature Hills, reaches 3–4 feet (1–1.2 m).

Caring for your live Japanese cedar tree isn't difficult, but you’ll want to limit how much time it spends indoors. Too much time in a warm house can make the tree unhappy. Indoors, keep the tree away from direct heat sources. When it’s time to take the tree outside, start it out in a sheltered spot or an unheated garage for a few days.

Be sure to keep the soil moist. Check it every day. Japanese cedars thrive in full sun to partial shade in USDA zones 5–9 and require well-drained, fertile soil. Standard varieties can grow to 50 feet (15 m) tall if planted in the ground. Dwarf cultivars stay much smaller.

You will recognize the lemon cypress (Cupressus macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’) – it’s the potted evergreen that you are likely to see in every store just before Christmas as a holiday plant. You can even get one from Walmart. It makes a charming, small Christmas tree with its natural pyramid shape, bright chartreuse foliage, and fresh citrus scent.

The lemon cypress is a versatile evergreen that, once the festive season is done, can be kept in a container on a patio in USDA zones 7–10. Be gentle with it indoors. Use lightweight ornaments since the soft branches can bend or break under heavier decorations. You’ll want to avoid hot lights, too. Use battery-operated micro fairy lights that don’t produce excess heat.

These trees grow slowly and can top out at 10 feet (3 m) tall and 3 feet (1 m) wide. Indoors, give them a sunny window with 6 hours of bright light a day. Keep the tree far from hot air vents and cool drafts, and provide a pebble tray for humidity. Transition the cypress to an outdoor location after the holidays.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7999. A November Garden Walk in Downtown Milwaukee

November is definitely settling in here in downtown Milwaukee, Wisconsin (Zone 6a). Most of the summer flowers are gone, leaves are piling up, and plenty of perennials are heading into dormancy. But there’s still so much to appreciate. Today we’re staying close to home for a walk around my neighborhood. I walk these streets with my dog all the time, and there are a handful of gardens I always slow down to admire.

Starting off strong with this one! This prairie-inspired garden is always buzzing with pollinators in summer, and it’s one of my favorites to walk by. In fall, the large sweeps of switchgrass (Panicum virgatum, Zones 4–9) and little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium, Zones 3–9) really come forward. And wow, those fluffy switchgrass plumes make a statement when planted en masse.

From the other side, the pinkish-copper tones of little bluestem become much more prominent. The planting even carries across the sidewalk into the curb strip, making this small garden pretty hard to miss.

A few houses down is another garden that inspires me. The whole yard is planted so elegantly, with interest no matter the season. Bare spaces are usually filled with annuals. But even in November, we still get to see roses in bloom and hydrangeas giving it their all to remain relevant. The urn in the background with the pumpkin is a lovely seasonal touch.

This garden might look messy to some, but this is the kind of fall mess I truly enjoy. The hostas (Hosta cvs., Zones 3–9) spilling over the stairs, surrounded and covered by fallen red maple leaves… I love it!

This deep burgundy shrub covered in bright red berries certainly caught my eye. Unfortunately, it’s Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii, Zones 4–8), an invasive shrub here in Wisconsin. If you like the look, consider one of these native alternatives to Japanese barberry, including chokeberry, fothergilla, Virginia sweetspire, summersweet, and inkberry.

This Siberian crab apple (Malus baccata, Zones 2–7) is absolutely covered in clusters of warm orange fruit. Once so many summer flowers have disappeared, fruiting trees like this become some of the strongest color in the landscape.

It’s nice to see another garden extend beyond the front yard and into the curb strip. These often-overlooked spaces have so much potential. They can become a small garden, pollinator planting, or even a bee lawn.

And, of course, who can resist a strip of marigolds (Tagetes cvs., annual)? Especially when they’re still looking this good!

And one final reminder to leave the leaves this fall! Fallen leaves provide important overwintering habitat for pollinators and other beneficial insects, so leaving some in garden beds gives them a place to shelter until spring.

Thanks for coming along on my afternoon walk! While I wish this were a fall update from my little concrete jungle of a backyard, it’s all packed up now… because I’m moving to Georgia in just a few short weeks! I’ll definitely miss these neighborhood gardens, but I’m excited to see what new gardens and plants catch my eye down South.

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Does your home’s landscape look barren and brown after autumn leaves fall, and doesn’t perk back up again until spring? Most homeowners think about how their beds will look when they’re in full bloom, but few imagine how that same bed will look in the dead of winter. Outdoor winter plants that add beautiful contrast to a snowy landscape aren’t just good for your curb appeal—they can also provide critical food sources and nesting sites for wildlife. As you consider updates to the plants and shrubs that surround your home, look to these appealing, year-round options.

Blue Ice bog rosemary’s unique silvery-blue foliage looks good in every season, plus this evergreen ground cover delights with a shock of pink bell-shaped blooms in early spring. Perfect for rock gardens and moist soils, it will attract birds and bring visual interest to the yard all year.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 6Size: 1 to 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Blue Ice Bog Rosemary at The Tree Center for $39.50

This dwarf pine variety turns from green to gold when cold weather arrives. In fact, the colder the climate, the more intense its color becomes. This rabbit- and deer-resistant plant is easy to care for, and an evergreen shrub that will look beautiful all year long. It grows slowly, but immediately adds low-growing color and texture to a winter bed.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 7Size: nearly 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted Carstens Wintergold Mugo Pine at Mike’s Plants on Etsy for $75

Many weeping ornamentals lose their leaves in cold weather, but not the weeping Norway spruce. With its unusual shape and showy cones, this evergreen makes a great accent in the garden and provides rich green in all four seasons. It can thrive in many soil types, including rich sandy soils, and has low water needs once established.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: 4 feet high and 15 feet aroundWhere to buy: Get a 3- to 4-foot high Weeping Norway Spruce at Spring Hill Nurseries for $299

This evergreen succulent creates a lush and attractive carpet that thrives year-round in cool to warm climates. Most boast tiny flowers that attract butterflies in summer, and the foliage of Pink Form and Purple Form can take on reddish to purple hues in colder months. Easy to care for in full sun, this little wonder packs a lot of life in its compact height but excellent spread. After a season or two, it is xeric.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 9Size: 1 feet high and 1 to 1.5 feet aroundWhere to buy: Get a 4-inch pot of Sedum Hispanicum at Cristina’s Garden on Etsy for $10.99

For evergreen ground cover in warmer climates, try Pot Belly Pittosporum. The tough little shrub flowers in spring and summer, leaving its silvery green foliage with a white underside on the plant through winter.  Best of all, it keeps its rounded shape with little maintenance required. Pot Belly Pittosporum is drought tolerant once established and can grow in partial to full sun.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 8 to 11Size: 4 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Pot Belly Pittosporum at Cornell Farm for $28.99

This ground-hugging variety of dianthus is evergreen and cold hardy. Its gray-green foliage erupts in summer with flowers, making it a wonderful filler both in the garden and in pots, so feel free to grow it in a container and overwinter it indoors in colder zones. The flowers are also fragrant, adding a clove-like scent to the garden.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: about 1 foot high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Frosty Fire Dianthus at Holly Days for $11.99

If you’re looking for a distinctive shade of evergreen color, dwarf globe blue spruce delivers. This slow-growing, densely branched conifer has blue needles that become more brilliant in summer. It makes a wonderful low hedge, or stands out as a small rabbit-resistant shrub.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 4 to 8Size: 2 to 3 feet high and 3 to 4 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Dwarf Globe Blue Spruce tree at Trees.com for $54.95

Pink pussytoe plants provide an evergreen mat of tiny silver-gray leaves. In late spring, the plant spikes deep pink, fuzzy flowers. It’s a slow grower and requires little water once established, so this cold-hardy beauty is a breeze to care for in any season. The native cultivar grows best in full sun.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: 0.5 feet high and 1 foot wideWhere to buy: Get a bag of 20 Pussytoes seeds at SeedCult on Etsy for $2.99

Snowdrop bulbs are happiest with cold or moderate winters, and are among favorite winter-flowering plants. Place them in full or partial where you can enjoy their delicate white flowers in the fall and throughout the cold months, even during snow. Come spring, they’ll go dormant.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 9Size: 0.5 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a bag of 25 Galanthus Nivalis bulbs at White Flower Farm for $20

Christmas rose, a variety of hellebore, is a pest-resistant evergreen perennial. It also provides valuable nectar for early pollinators, like the rusty patched bumblebee, who are seeking blooms in late winter or early spring. Find it a shady location with space to grow, and soon you’ll enjoy its white winter blooms in the warmer end of their growing range or early spring where colder.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: 1 foot tall and up to 1.5 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted Ivory Prince Christmas Rose at Plant Addicts for $49.99

Winter jasmine is a vining shrub that will treat you with bursts of fragrant yellow flowers between late winter and early spring; the plant’s flowers often are the first to appear as winter wraps up. But even when not in bloom, this plant’s large arching stems will provide plenty of visual interest to the garden. Hardy and easy to grow, winter jasmine is just at home in coastal areas as it is along rock walls.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 10Size: up to 10 feet tall and 6 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon pot of Winter Jasmine at The Home Depot for $25.58

Known for its medicinal properties, witch hazel is often used in cosmetics and lotions, since it is reported to reduce inflammation and soothe certain skin irritations. It’s also a great choice for a winter garden, thanks to its fragrant yellow-to-red flowers that can bloom even in snowy weather. This adaptable shrub or small tree thrives in full sun to partial shade.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: 3 to 6 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1- to 2-foot high Witch Hazel at TN Nursery for $26.99

Named for its small clusters of white berries that put on a show throughout the winter and give way to little white flowers in the spring, the snowberry plant provides a valuable food source for birds during the cold winter months. This easy-care plant will spread as a dense thicket, so it’s a great choice for borders and living fences.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 9Size: more than 15 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted White Snowberry at The Home Depot for $38.04

Featuring dark green glossy leaves, sweet box plants are shade-loving evergreen shrubs that boast small fragrant flowers that bloom in late winter and early spring. Once the fragrant flowers fade, little black fruits will appear in their wake. Preferring partial to full shade, sweet box plants are tough and excellent year-round plants to add interest to the garden.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 8Size: up to 2 feet high and 4 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Fragrant Dwarf Sweet Box at Planting Partners on Etsy for $28.99

For a vibrant splash of color in warmer zones, plant winter heath in your yard, which will repay you with abundant tiny pink winter flowers that bloom in late winter through early spring. The colorful winter shrub is an even hardier version of E. carnea, and both are commonly used as a ground cover, forming a dense mat. Prune it right after it finishes flowering in the spring to prevent leafless stems and keep it looking great all year.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 8Size: up to 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a quart-size potted Erica Kramer’s Red Winter Heath at The Home Depot for $18.53

This deciduous shrub’s large size creates a show-stopping garden accent. In mid- to late fall, the American cranberry bush will burst with vibrant red berries that last into winter. The berries  are edible but aren’t very tasty when eaten raw. However, they provide important winter food for wildlife. Fragrant while flowers appear in spring and persist through mid summer. The shrub thrives in full or partial sun and prefers alkaline soil.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 7Size: 8 to 12 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 3-gallon Bailey Compact American Cranberry Bush at Plant Addicts for $73.99

Also known as Perovskia, Russian sage is popular for its tall blue-violet flowers that bloom in the summer through the fall, attracting all sorts of pollinators to the garden. However, this shrub looks great in the winter, too, thanks to long silvery stems that offer structure and intrigue to a winter landscape. Leave the faded flower stems on until new growth appears in spring and plant Russian sage along walkways to maximize enjoyment of its fragrant flowers in summer. Once established, it is a drought-tolerant shrub.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 9Size: up to 4 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 3-inch potted Lacey Blue Russian Sage at American Meadows for $7.99

Also known as Eastern teaberry, American wintergreen features glossy evergreen leaves and bright red berries that will offer a beautiful contrast to a wintery white landscape. Like many winter outdoor plants, this shrub helps small mammals and birds who love the berries. It is disease-resistant, and crushing its leaves will release a refreshing wintergreen scent. Plant the showy low grower in dappled sunlight to deep shade to keep it happy.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: less than 1 foot high and up to 1 foot wideWhere to buy: Get 6 bare root Teaberry Wintergreen plants at New Hampshire Plants on Etsy for $9.99

Yucca glauca is among the most winter-hardy yucca varieties. Its attractive evergreen foliage features long narrow stems in a rosette shape that look great all year long. In the spring, a stem rises from the rosette that features white bell-shaped flowers. These flowers attract butterflies, and the entire easy-care yucca plant provides food and nesting opportunities for small mammals, birds, and reptiles.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 4 to 8Size: 3 to 4 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 5-inch pot of Soapweed Yucca at Etsy for $24.75

This low-growing shrub features glossy dark green leaves that turn bronze in the fall, persisting through the winter. During the winter you’ll also be treated to the shrub’s remaining vivid red berries, which provide a valuable food source for birds. The berries arise from tiny white flowers that form in the spring and summer, which butterflies love. Plant it in full sun to watch it thrive, though the shrub can handle partial shade.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 8Size: 1 foot high and 4 to 6 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Bearberry Cotoneaster Coral Beauty at Plants Express for $17.95

The prices listed here are accurate as of publication on November 3, 2026.

#7997. ISIS-Inspired Terrorist Sentenced for Attacking Guards While Serving Sentence for Separate NYC Terror Plot

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, of Ontario, Canada, was sentenced today to 50 years in prison for offenses related to a 2020 attack on correctional officers at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood. This sentence will run consecutive to the 40-year sentence he is currently serving for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS.

“Bahnasawy, who is already serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for plotting mass casualty attacks in New York City on behalf of ISIS, savagely attacked corrections officers once again on behalf of ISIS,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”

“We will prosecute those who aid, attempt to aid, or commit violence on behalf of the pernicious ISIS ideology wherever they may be found,” said U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. “Today’s sentence reflects our unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of ISIS even behind prison walls.”

“Although he was behind bars, this convicted terrorist committed a horrific attack on two corrections officers in the name of ISIS, which they fortunately survived,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “Today’s sentencing shows that violent attacks by those who support the evil ideology of ISIS or other foreign terrorist organizations cannot be tolerated by our society. Fighting terrorism is a central part of the FBI’s mission to protect the American people, and the FBI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to hold these vicious criminals accountable.”

Bahnasawy was an inmate at USP Allenwood who, on Dec. 7, 2020, attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. Bahnasawy stabbed one officer in the head and face, and, when a second responded to assist, Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand.

The first officer eventually lost his right eye as a result of the attack. When Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was found in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) was also found taped to the inside of a locker door in Bahnasawy’s prison cell. Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization.

At the time of the attacks at USP Allenwood, Bahnasawy was serving a 40-year sentence for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS. Bahnasawy, a then-20-year-old Canadian citizen and resident, plotted with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City during the Islamic holy month of Ramadhan in 2016, all in the name of ISIS.

An undercover FBI agent (UC) infiltrated the co-conspirators’ terrorist plot, posing as an ISIS supporter prepared to join in the attacks. The FBI arrested Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he traveled from Canada to the New York City area in preparation for the attacks, and he has been in custody since that time.

This case was investigated by the FBI’s Philadelphia Field Office.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey MacArthur for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and Deputy Chief Larry Schneider of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section prosecuted the case.

As the season changes and winter approaches, it’s time to prepare your garden for colder months. Prepping beds and plants in fall keeps your landscape tidy and gives you a jump start on spring by creating the ideal growing environment for those long-awaited annual flower and veggie plants. So, put your garden to bed, and let both you and your landscape rest easy over winter with these essential tasks.

Although hydrangea flowerheads can look pretty framed against a winter landscape, it’s important not to leave them to their own devices this month. Make a little time in November for these care essentials

A few thoughtful changes will keep your garden landscape looking effortlessly stylish through the cooler seasons.

Zipping tender shrubs into plant covers keeps them cozy over winter, and here's everything you need to know to choose the right one for your zone.

Keeping a bird bath ice-free could mean life or death for your garden birds this winter.

Those gorgeous flowers are months away, but their buds are already waiting. The right fall care can make all the difference when warmer days return.

Waterlogged soil is the prime reason potted plants fail in fall and winter, and this speedy solution couldn't be simpler.

Treat your clematis vine to some TLC in fall and your stronger, healthier plant will sail through the cold season to bring abundant blooms next year.

Don’t get too dazzled by this season’s fabulous show of dahlia flowers because you need to start preparing tubers for winter to enjoy even bigger blooms next year.

#7995. Winter Container Inspiration From New Jersey

Hi GPOD! Today we’re returning to New Jersey to see more from Ellen Goldfarb and Tracy Buttrick. After sharing their beautiful fall containers with us, Ellen is back with some winter inspiration using colorful branches, evergreens, berries, pinecones, and more.

This beautiful antique lead planter in Ridgewood, New Jersey, always calls for a generous amount of greenery and nice height. We try to change what we do from year to year. This time we used curly willow, artificial white berry picks, magnolia leaves, red winterberry (Ilex verticillata, Zones 3–9), and frosted pinecones. Silver bell eucalyptus, silver brunia stems, noble fir (Abies procera, Zones 5–6), and incense cedar (Calocedrus decurrens, Zones 5–8) fill out the arrangement.

This is the same antique planter and house as in the previous photo, but from another winter. That year we used a combination of yellow twig dogwood (Cornus sericea ‘Flaviramea’, Zones 3–7) and red twig dogwood (Cornus sericea cvs., Zones 2–7) for lots of winter color. We also used artificial berry picks in pink and white and natural brown pine cones.

We like to use real berries, but sometimes the birds eat them before the season ends. Artificial berries give the client guaranteed color for longer. For greenery, we used desert juniper (Juniperus osteosperma, Zones 3–9), balsam fir (Abies balsamea, Zones 3–6), and incense cedar.

This slim planter sits on a small sliver of a step at an entry in Ho-Ho-Kus, New Jersey. It is simple but one of my favorites, with stunning red twig dogwood stems. We buy these from a farm that also grows and sells the more common darker-red stems.

Beneath the red is a froth of desert juniper. Dried lotus pods (Nelumbo cvs., Zones 4–10) and clusters of silver brunia punctuate the greenery. The finishing touch is a frilly skirt of bright chartreuse incense cedar.

This one sounds like an outfit, doesn’t it?

One of a pair of pots on the front porch of a Mission-style house in Teaneck, New Jersey, these had plenty of space for tall branches. We liked the combination of golden curly willow (Salix matsudana ‘Tortuosa’, Zones 4–8) and redtwig dogwood against the creamy tan stucco.

We tucked in shiny magnolia leaves with taller silver bell eucalyptus, then added natural brown pinecones and small clumps of silver brunia. A generous, draping swath of incense cedar finishes the bottom of the arrangement.

This is a window box in Englewood, New Jersey. A classic house calls for a classic planting. We used red winterberries, magnolia leaves, frosted pinecones, and silver brunia clusters. Some noble fir and our favorite evergreen, incense cedar, finish the arrangement.

This is a close-up detail of a planter in Franklin Lakes, New Jersey. Dark red twig dogwood stems are mixed with curly willow and branches of multiflora rose hips. We love using the rose hips, but they are sometimes hard to find.

This pot also had artificial white berry picks and Eastern white pine (Pinus strobus, Zones 3–8). Silver brunia on longer stems, noble fir, and incense cedar complete the arrangement.

Thank you for sharing more of your beautiful container designs with us, Ellen and Tracy! I love seeing how many different looks can come from a relatively small palette of winter materials. Changing the color and shape of the branches, berries, cones, and evergreens gives each container its own personality.

We have even more of Ellen and Tracy’s winter containers to share, so we’ll be back tomorrow with another round of inspiration!
