#7911. 6 Tricks to Get Back Into Your House After Getting Locked Out

Updated Nov 6, 2026 11:53 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Q: Last night I was almost locked out of the house, as I nearly left my keys on the counter before walking to a neighborhood BBQ. That got me thinking—what should I have done if I locked myself out of my house? And are there steps I can take to make sure it never happens? I’m thinking of giving a spare key to a neighbor, but I’m unsure what else can be done!

A: Getting locked out of your house can be a frustrating experience, but it’s not as uncommon as you may think. And unless you’re prepared, the situation can be more terrifying than it has to be.

Thankfully, there are plenty of ways to get back inside a house without breaking in through your door, even if all signs point to the opposite. From checking windows or removing door knobs to calling a locksmith or family member with a spare key, there’s no shortage of options at your disposal. Once you get back inside, you can then take steps to protect yourself from getting locked out again. This includes installing smart locks or hiding a key in a secure location somewhere else on your property.

If your door lock is locked and you’re outside the home, the first thing to do is stay calm. It’s easy to panic, but there are several ways to remedy the situation. Here’s a look at actions you can take to get back inside.

The quickest way to get back inside a home when locked out of the house with no key is by searching for another door or window that may be unlocked. Whether it’s a back door or basement window, be sure to check all entryways that are reasonably accessible. This might mean removing or damaging a window screen, but if it’s the difference between being locked outside and getting back inside, that’s a small price to pay. If there’s no easy way to get to the second-story windows, it’s best to leave them be—there are plenty of other ways to get inside, so there’s no reason to risk an injury.

If a family member, friend, or neighbor has a spare key, now is the time to try and contact them. People locked out of their homes who still have their smartphones with them can place a quick call to the owner of their spare. If the cell phone is inside the house, consider asking a neighbor or walking to a local shop and using their phone. This won’t be possible in all locations (especially in rural areas), but it’s a nice backup if a smartphone isn’t readily available. At any rate, contacting the person responsible for the spare key should be a top priority.

Individuals locked out of a rental unit can contact either their landlord or the maintenance company to help get back inside. The landlord will almost certainly have a spare key. If the rental unit is part of a large apartment building, there’s likely a maintenance technician on site who can help instead of the landlord. Many apartments also have a leasing office, so if someone is locked out of an apartment and doesn’t have the contact details for maintenance or their landlord, they can try this location as a backup. Most leasing offices are staffed during normal business hours and are more than willing to help tenants locked outside their apartments.

Though it’s not easy, attempting to pick the lock is worth consideration. Some door latches can be reached with a twisted paper clip or credit card. To attempt this, the card or paper clip needs to slip past the strike plate and catch the door latch. Once the latch is caught, it can be pushed out of place and the door can be opened. If the deadbolt is in place, this technique will not work. But if it’s just a simple latch on a door knob, it’s certainly worth a try. Unlocking a door this way is tricky, though it may be effective in some situations.

Another possible way to get back inside is to remove the door knob. This requires users to have access to a standard toolkit, though often just a screwdriver can get the job done. Most knobs don’t have exposed screws on their exterior plate, but it’s possible to gain access to them by looking for a small slot somewhere else on its faceplate. This small slot keeps the knob and faceplate in place—by depressing it, users can remove the faceplate and gain access to the screws.

With the screws exposed, they can be loosened and the door knob can be removed. This gives access to the lock’s inner workings, part of which includes a mechanism for opening the door. Try using a screwdriver to twist the inner component, which should unlock the latch. Keep in mind these general steps won’t work for all types of locks, as each model is unique. For detailed steps, it’s a good idea to look up installation instructions for the specific brand in question.

The simplest way to unlock a locked door is by contacting a locksmith. These trained professionals can not only circumvent a locked door, but they’re trained to also repair or replace the lock once the door is open. The process typically doesn’t take very long, with many home lockout services lasting no more than an hour.

Pricing for locksmiths varies by location, but in an emergency situation, they’re worth every penny. Many locksmiths deal with more than just residential homes, making them a great choice when locked out of a car, RV, or any other building. They can even rekey a lock and help people locked out with the key stuck in the door. They are also trained to assist with changing locks on the door if an upgrade or replacement is required. So if none of the above steps work, a locksmith offering house lockout service is the best option.

While accidents can happen to anyone, there are steps people can take to prevent future house lockouts. This includes simple things like hiding a spare key somewhere around the property and giving a spare to a neighbor, along with more complicated tasks like installing smart locks. Not all of these steps will apply to all homes, but the more failsafes in place, the better the odds of getting back inside.

Installing one of the best security systems (such as Vivint or ADT) is a great way to keep burglars at bay and improve home security. If the system also includes a smart lock, users have a quick way to get back inside when locked out. In fact, many smart locks are designed in a way that makes it nearly impossible to get locked out, as they can be controlled with a physical key or the built-in keypad.

With a traditional lock, leaving the key inside the home results in a lockout. With a smart lock, leaving the key inside simply means users need to use their digital code to get back inside. Some of the best smart locks, like the Yale Assure Lock 2, also work with mobile companion apps, letting users open the door with their smartphone.

Alternatively, many of the best electronic door locks toe the line between traditional and smart locks, making them a good choice for homes looking for the best of both worlds. It’s important to read up on what smart locks are before making a purchase, as well as learn about the types of door locks available, as there are advantages and disadvantages to them all.

While shopping for a security system and smart lock, homeowners can also pick up other security gear, including the best door security bars to help prevent break-ins.

Giving a key to a trusted neighbor or nearby family member is a simple (yet effective) way to prevent getting locked out. Ideally, this will be someone easy to reach and within walking distance of the home, ensuring they can quickly get to the home without requiring a phone call or a long drive.

However, it’s important to have complete trust in the person receiving the spare key. Not only can they help during lockouts, but they can essentially enter the home whenever they’d like. This makes it important to only pass out spare keys to neighbors who have proven themselves to be responsible and trustworthy. Otherwise, this step could result in more headaches than it’s worth.

Hiding a spare key on the property is another popular way to ensure lockouts never happen, but this needs to be handled with care. Ideally, a lock box with a spare key inside will be installed near the front door, allowing only people with the password access to the spare. This is leagues better than simply hiding a key under the doormat or inside a yard decoration, as anyone who stumbles upon the key will be able to get into the home.

If a lockbox isn’t used, then ensure that the hidden spare key is in a location that won’t be disturbed by harsh weather or easily seen by prying eyes. This includes inside a dog house, under a brick or patio paver, inside a magnetic holder placed under a bench, or stowed away inside a fake rock. Poor locations to hide a key include under a doormat, under a flowerpot, or on top of the door frame.

Keeping a spare key in a wallet or purse comes with serious drawbacks. For one, if the wallet or purse is lost, someone will now have a key to the home, meaning it’s best to have the lock rekeyed. If the key is placed in a purse or wallet without a way to keep it secure, it’s also possible for it to slip out while reaching for a credit card or cash. Because of this, anyone storing a key in their wallet or purse will need to invest in a key holder—these are cheap, secure, and prevent the key from rubbing against the wall of the wallet and piercing its side.

The benefits of keeping a spare key in a wallet or purse may outweigh the drawbacks, especially for people who never leave home without their purse or wallet. This essentially gives individuals another way to get back inside their home without requiring their keychain.

The simplest way to prevent a lockout is to get in the habit of never leaving home without a set of keys. This is easier said than done, but certain actions help turn this into a routine. Many people prefer to place a dish or tray near their front door for valuables like their keys. When leaving the home, having the keys right next to the exit makes it virtually impossible to forget them. Other people like to use a keychain that’s visually appealing, ensuring it catches their eyes when leaving the home.

Aside from making the keys easy to spot when leaving, good habits include reserving a specific pocket for keys, checking for keys before closing any lockable door, and communicating with family members or roommates to ensure they don’t get locked out if no one else is home.

Getting locked out of the house can be a frightening experience. Thankfully, there are several ways to remedy the situation and get back inside. From asking a neighbor for a spare and checking for unlocked windows to calling a locksmith or attempting to pick the lock, there’s an option that works for everyone.

The best option is to prevent lockouts from happening in the first place. To that end, installing smart locks and stashing a spare key on the property are both great options. Each home will have techniques that work better than others, and it’s up to each individual to determine what works best for them.

#7910. Crime in Texas, Trial in Texas, Confession to Clergy in North Carolina: Which Law Applies?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

By design, our American legal system largely lets different states make different rules. Most states recognize a tort of disclosure of private facts; some don't. A few recognize a tort of alienation of affections; most don't. Some states allow first-cousin marriage; others don't. Some set a one-year statute of limitations for defamation; some set it at two or three years. The list goes on.

Much conduct happens in one state, and the resulting disputes arise in the courts of that state. But other matters are multi-state affairs. Indeed, some are multinational affairs, even though they end up in one country's courts: What happens if a contract was entered into in France, performed in Canada, but plaintiff sues defendant over an alleged breach where they now both live, in Illinois?

There is therefore a body of law called "conflict of laws" (or "choice of laws") that tries to resolve these questions. As it happens, that is itself state law, so different states can have different conflicts rules, with at least three major schools of thought on the matter. (Think that's confusing? Don't get me started on renvoi and dépeçage.)

Here's a scenario that arose in the recent Texas Campbell v. State case:

Appellant was charged, in Harris County, Texas, with murdering his girlfriend. His girlfriend was killed in Texas. And then Appellant went to his mother's home in North Carolina.

While he was in North Carolina, Appellant's mother urged Appellant to speak with a bishop on the telephone. While he was on the phone with the bishop, and allegedly with his mother still in the room, Appellant made a statement admitting that he killed his girlfriend. During trial, the bishop was called to testify as a witness about the contents of Appellant's statement….

Texas Rule of Evidence 505(b) sets forth a clergy-penitent testimonial privilege:

A communicant has a privilege to refuse to disclose and to prevent any other person from disclosing a confidential communication by the communicant to a clergy member in the clergy member's professional capacity as a spiritual advisor.

{[A communication is] "confidential" if made privately and not intended for further disclosure except to other persons present to further the purpose of the communication.}

But though all states have some clergy-penitent privilege, North Carolina courts have interpreted the N.C. privilege statute as not applying "when the disclosures are made in the presence of a third party," apparently with no exception (as in Texas and some other states) for people "present to further the purpose of the communication."

Gonzalez v. State (2001), a precedent from the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals (Texas's highest court for criminal laws) relied on the Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws and its "most significant relationship test" when determining which state's law applies. (The Restatement is an influential work compiled by the American Law Institute, a generally highly respected organization of lawyers, judges, and academics; many courts find it persuasive, as the Texas court did in Gnozalez.)

And the court concluded, citing the comments to the Restatement, "that the state where the communication took place is generally the state with the most significant relationship." Based on that precedent, a Texas appellate court in Campbell held that North Carolina law applied, and that the communication was admissible.

But Texas Court of Criminal Appeals Judge Kevin Yeary took a different view dissenting from denial of review in September:

[T]he Restatement is not the law of this state. When our Texas Rules of Evidence were adopted, this state did not incorporate language from the Restatement demanding that a different rule should apply when a clergy-communicant statement is made outside of our state's borders.

There is also no textual basis for any argument that any conflict between the laws of another state and our state's Rules of Evidence should be considered. Our state's rule on clergy-communications contains no exception for circumstances in which such a communication occurs in a different state. There appears to be no true legal reason to even dwell on such a question, unless perhaps a court just does not like our rule of evidence!

We are not bound by the Restatements of the Laws. We should not consider ourselves to be controlled by them in any regard. We should also not consider ourselves, or our lower courts, to be at liberty to simply adopt any Restatement as the law of this state, even if we think it has expressed a good idea.

Judges are not elected to play the role of policy makers. If anyone in this state thinks we should change a rule or a policy expressed in a rule, then that person should raise the matter as a proposed change to our Texas Rules of Evidence. In that way, the matter could be considered by a rules committee, and the committee could then consider public input before deciding whether to amend our rule.

We have rules of evidence that are written down, with pesky little things called words—that mean things. Presumably, the people who adopted our Texas Rules of Evidence fully considered them, and the words in them, before adopting them. We should consider whether the words in our actual rules are enough….

On its own terms, the rule is quite clear. It does not contemplate the situation in which the statement is made to clergy when the communicant is out of state. When our courts, and when we, pretend that our rule of evidence demands a different set of rules for when a communication occurs in another state, we destroy our own credibility as an equal arbiter of the law. Our courts should simply follow the language of our own Rules. And we should lead the lower courts in that direction by granting review in this case to show them the way….

Under Texas Rule of Evidence Rule 505(a)(3), Appellant's mother's presence might not serve to preclude Appellant from asserting the clergy-communicant privilege. It is therefore conceivable that, if the Texas Rule had been applied, Appellant might have been able to prevent the bishop from testifying.

The Restatement (Second) of Conflicts of Law § 139 (1) states: "(1) Evidence that is not privileged under the local law of the state which has the most significant relationship with the communication will be admitted, even though it would be privileged under the local law of the forum, unless the admission of such evidence would be contrary to the strong public policy of the forum." It is seems to me that there exist strong arguments that allowing the admission of the communication at issue in this case is against the strong public policy of Texas. By its own terms, Texas's clergy-communicant privilege can even apply when made in the presence of a third person; and Texas rule makers certainly added this section intentionally. Tex. R. Evid. 505(a)(3) ("A communication is 'confidential' if made privately and not intended for further disclosure except to other persons present to further the purpose of the communication.") We should look for the "strong public policy" of the state in the plain text of the rule.

I should note that the subject of conflicts of law is largely about deciding when a foreign law should be used even when a local statute would on its face appear to apply. The theory is that legislatures generally write statutes with an eye towards local matters, and can't be expected to consider all the complications that arise in the rare multi-state cases; better leave that to courts to figure out using judge-made choice-of-law rules, the theory goes. But Judge Yeary argues that courts ought to take a more textualist approach to such questions.

I'm inclined towards the choice-of-law rule applied in Gonzalez, under which courts should apply the law of the place where the communication happened. (Of course, that can still leave a question of what happens if the communication is by Zoom, and the clergy member is in one state and the congregant is in another.) But in any event, I thought this was an interesting question to pass along.

#7909. What Is “Heart Attack Snow,” and Why Is It So Dangerous?

Heavy, wet snow can turn an ordinary winter chore into a health risk. Learn why people call it heart attack snow and how to shovel safely.

Shoveling snow can be a dangerous winter chore. Icy walkways can cause serious falls, and prolonged exposure to the cold can lead to hypothermia or frostbite. Another safety concern is something called “heart attack snow.”

The name sounds dramatic, but it points to a real concern for people clearing sidewalks and driveways in winter. For those in snowy climates, understanding the risks of heart attack snow is important before picking up a shovel.

Understanding the risks can help prevent a routine chore from becoming a medical emergency.

Heart attack snow is a nickname for heavy, wet snow that’s harder to shovel than dry, powdery snow. The name comes from the strain that lifting this type of snow can place on the heart. According to the National Weather Service, snow with a higher water content weighs more, making each shovelful harder to lift.

The added effort can quickly raise heart rate and blood pressure. Cold temperatures also cause blood vessels to narrow, making the heart work harder. The American Heart Association warns that this combination can trigger a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest.

The association says the risks are especially concerning for “people who already have cardiovascular risks like a sedentary lifestyle or obesity,” including those with a history of smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, or high blood pressure. People who have previously suffered a heart attack or stroke also face greater risks.

Even lighter, powdery snow can be dangerous, especially when large amounts require repeated lifting or hours of clearing.

Before heading outside, people should warm up indoors and stretch gently. Dressing in layers helps protect against the cold, while staying hydrated is important even when someone doesn’t feel thirsty.

The American Heart Association recommends pushing snow rather than lifting it whenever possible. When lifting is necessary, smaller loads and frequent breaks can help limit physical strain. A snow blower can also reduce the amount of lifting, although operating one still requires effort.

Slippery surfaces are another concern. “Walking on ice is extremely dangerous,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The agency recommends using rock salt or another de-icing product to keep walkways clear of ice. Sand can also help prevent slipping.

People with heart disease or significant cardiovascular risk factors should have someone else handle snow removal, according to the American Heart Association.

Recognizing the warning signs of a heart attack is equally important. Chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, cold sweats, or discomfort in the arms, back, or jaw can all signal a serious problem. Symptoms aren’t always severe and can vary from person to person.

Anyone experiencing possible heart attack symptoms should stop shoveling immediately and call 911. The American Heart Association advises against waiting to see whether symptoms go away.

American Heart Association, “Snow Shoveling, Cold Temperatures Combine for Perfect Storm of Heart Health Hazards” American Heart Association, “Warning Signs of a Heart Attack” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Preparedness” Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm”

#7907. Court Dismisses Claims Over Alleged "Doxing" and Criticism of Homelessness / Needle Exchange Activists

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Stabbin Wagon v. City of Medford, decided Sept. 30 by Judge Mustafa Kasubhai (D. Ore.):

The Court assumes the following alleged facts are true. Stabbin' Wagon is a Medford non-profit that provides clean needles, food and aid, and outreach services to unhoused people, particularly those suffering from drug addiction and mental illnesses. Plaintiff Jones was the founder and executive director of Stabbin' Wagon and Plaintiff Strong was an employee. Plaintiffs frequently criticized the City's arrests of unhoused individuals and its failure to provide outreach services to those individuals.

Defendants Brian Sjothun, Randy Sparacino, Justin Ivens, Darrel Graham, Geoff Kirkpatrick, Trevor Arnold, Arturo Vega, and John and Jane Does (collectively, "City Defendants") are current and former Medford city officials and police officers. City Defendants have criticized Plaintiffs and their needle exchange program. Starting around 2021, Defendants Graham, Kirkpatrick, and Sparacino monitored the Plaintiffs' social media activities, protest attendance, and interviews with newspapers. City Defendants removed Plaintiffs from police communications which alerted local outreach services when the police swept an encampment of unhoused individuals. Medford police have also stopped, arrested, and cited Stabbin' Wagon employees on several occasions from 2020 to 2023.

In 2023, Plaintiffs received a $1.5 million grant from the Oregon Health Authority ("OHA") to open a 'respite center' to provide more outreach services to unhoused people. Defendants Sjothun, Ivens, Arnold, and Kirkpatrick attempted to persuade OHA to rescind the grant. Plaintiffs allege that these Defendants "disseminated inflammatory, false, and disparaging information about Plaintiffs to other providers, state officials, and community leaders" in their attempt to reverse the grant.

Defendant Ryan Mallory is "a law-enforcement-adjacent figure in Southern Oregon" who operates social media platforms and companies that investigate, report, and consult on matters related to law enforcement, including the Medford Police Department. Defendant Mallory supported City Defendants' attempt to rescind the grant. He expressed his opposition to Plaintiffs' OHA grant on his Facebook group which has over 100,000 followers. His followers commented in support, and on September 13, 2023, one approached Plaintiffs while they were working and threatened to call the police. On August 4, 2023, Defendant Mallory posted Plaintiffs' personal information, including their home addresses and birthdays, in a graphic with Plaintiffs' likenesses resembling "law enforcement booking records." On September 7, 2023, Defendant Mallory posted a video and a comment that urged the public to oppose the OHA grant, stating in part:

Unqualified people that fill our Parks in greenways with needles, keep people addicted by promoting drug use, and misappropriate grant money by using it for public protest of the police rather than helping people are about to get a massive paycheck …. Ask for an audit of the stabbin wagon organization…. These folks are intending on renting a building to perpetuate drug use …. Melissa Jones and her marketing director [Sam Strong] have openly stated that they get grant money and use it to protest police and others.

Defendant Mallory and his followers continued making posts that "fomented animosity and disinformation regarding Plaintiffs and their services." On May 21, 2024, Defendant Mallory posted an article that discussed Plaintiff Jones's sentencing in municipal court and commented that she "[d]efinitely hasn't learned her lesson based on that. Guess we'll see how probation goes." In March 2025, Defendant Mallory posted a video that showed needles on the ground in downtown Medford and commented that Stabbin' Wagon "shouldn't be in business at all, it worsens the problem."

OHA delayed Plaintiffs' grant but ultimately awarded the funds. "[M]unicipal and zoning barriers and Defendants' subversion campaign" forced Plaintiffs to end their attempt to open the respite center. Plaintiffs Jones and Strong resigned from Stabbin' Wagon due to the Defendants' "harassment, surveillance, doxing, and retaliatory pressure." …

The court dismissed plaintiffs' claims (which related to doxing, criticism, surveillance, and retaliation) on various grounds, including that they were filed too late, but also added this:

Plaintiffs also allege that Defendants retaliated against Plaintiffs advocacy by opposing their grant from OHA and publicly and privately disparaging them. Plaintiffs allege that immediately after OHA awarded Stabbin' Wagon the grant, the City and Medford police, including Defendants Sjothun, Ivens, Arnold, and Kirkpatrick disseminated false and misleading information to state officials, community leaders, and other organizations. Plaintiffs allege the City sought to portray Stabbin' Wagon as extreme and unqualified, lobbied OHA, and coordinated with other nonprofits hostile to Stabbin' Wagon like OnTrack Rogue Valley and the Addictions Recovery Center.

Courts take a cautious approach with retaliation claims involving government speech like those here.

Restricting the ability of government decisionmakers to engage in speech risks interfering with their ability to effectively perform their duties. It also ignores the competing First Amendment rights of the officials themselves. The First Amendment is intended to "preserve an uninhibited marketplace of ideas in which truth will ultimately prevail." That marketplace of ideas is undermined if public officials are prevented from responding to speech of citizens with speech of their own.

The Ninth Circuit has accordingly set a high bar for when government speech gives rise to a First Amendment retaliation claim. For example, an act of defamation does not give rise to a retaliation claim if it does not affect the plaintiff's rights, benefits, or status with the state. Government speech that results in reputational harm and ultimately a loss in employment also does not meet the high bar for adverse action….

False accusations may give rise to a retaliation claim in certain contexts, however. In Mendocino Env't Ctr. v. Mendocino County (9th Cir. 1999), police officers falsely accused members of an environmental organization of criminal activity in connection with a criminal investigation. The officers made false accusations to secure arrest and search warrants. The Ninth Circuit held that plaintiffs sufficiently alleged a First Amendment retaliation claim because the inclusion of the accusations in warrant affidavits permitted the inference that the acts would chill a person of ordinary firmness from future first amendment activities.

At the outset, some of Plaintiffs' allegations fail because they seek to hold Defendants accountable for protected speech. For example, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants Ivens and Arnold "expressed outrage over the award and attempted to mobilize public opposition and influence OHA to rescind the grant." They also allege that the City portrayed "Stabbin' Wagon as untrustworthy, unqualified, and politically extreme." These allegations are insufficient to give rise to Plaintiffs' retaliation claim because the government must be allowed to express its own views, even when it is critical of some of its citizens….

Plaintiffs [also] allege that OHA delayed Stabbin' Wagon's grant in response to Defendants' conduct but ultimately awarded it. Plaintiffs Jones and Strong resigned from Stabbin' Wagon and Plaintiffs had to close their peer respite program. Plaintiffs, however, do not allege that Defendants had any control over the grant process and conceded that point at oral argument. This is fatal to Plaintiffs' allegations that Defendants "disseminated inflammatory, false, and disparaging information about Plaintiffs." Cf. Gini v. Las Vegas Metro. Police Dep't (9th Cir. 1994) (holding defamatory statements did not give rise to a First Amendment violation where the officials "could not, and did not, make any decision or take any state action affecting [the plaintiff's] rights, benefits, relationship or status with the state")….

And the court had this to say about plaintiffs' civil rights conspiracy claim:

A plaintiff bringing a Section 1985 claim to vindicate rights secured by the First Amendment must "prove that the state was somehow involved in or affected by the conspiracy" because the First Amendment "restrains only official conduct." Plaintiffs remaining allegations are that unspecified Defendants coordinated "with anti-activist social media groups that published private information and incited public backlash" and disseminated "Plaintiffs' private identifying information, obtained through law enforcement channels, to more than 100,000 followers in order to incite harassment and vigilantism against Plaintiffs."

Plaintiffs make numerous allegations attributing this conduct to Defendant Mallory who is not a City official. Much of Plaintiffs' allegations center on Defendant Mallory's speech via social media and other outlets. Digital communications like these generally fall within the First Amendment's protections. Speech is generally protected unless it falls into a category of unprotected speech [such as the category of "true threats"]. Some of these allegations seek to impose liability for protected speech and therefore fail. E.g., SAC [Second Amended Comalaint] ¶ 121 (alleging Defendant Mallory criticized Plaintiffs' qualifications). Plaintiffs summarily allege categories of potentially unprotected speech by Defendant Mallory. E.g., SAC ¶¶ 129, 131 (alleging Plaintiffs experienced harassment); SAC (alleging defamatory statements); SAC ¶ 203.e (incitement). To the extent Plaintiffs seek to hold Defendant Mallory liable for these acts, Plaintiffs must identify the alleged unprotected speech with more specificity and without relying on broad legal conclusions.

Plaintiffs also allege Defendant Mallory published Plaintiffs' names and home addresses in a "[b]usted" graphic, mimicking booking log services. A party generally cannot maintain a claim for disclosure of publicly available information that is lawfully obtained. Florida Star v. B.J.F. (1989). Plaintiffs do not allege their names and home addresses were not publicly available or unlawfully obtained. Plaintiffs therefore have not alleged an overt act by Defendant Mallory.

With respect to the City Defendants, Plaintiffs allege that the "City Defendants, in particular the members of the Medford Police Department, were aware of Defendant Mallory's pro-law enforcement social media influence." Plaintiffs further allege that Defendants Kirkpatrick and Sparacino appeared on Defendant Mallory's podcast. Plaintiff makes the general allegation that "Defendants … reached a tacit understanding that Defendant Mallory would" amplify the City Defendants' retaliation against Plaintiffs.

Viewed in light of the Court's rulings above, these allegations are insufficient to allege the participation of the City Defendants in the alleged disclosure of Plaintiffs' personal information. A plaintiff must allege a conspiracy with facts that rise above allegations of parallel conduct and sympathetic viewpoints. Plaintiffs' general allegation of tacit agreement is insufficient. The Court has found that Plaintiffs have not adequately alleged the City Defendants retaliated against them, so Defendant Mallory cannot be said to have amplified it at this time. Plaintiffs' Section 1985(3) claim is dismissed because they must allege that "two or more persons conspire[d]" and that a state actor is "at least one of the wrongdoers." …

Stephanie C. Kucera and Zachariah H. Allen (Hart Wagner LLP) and Casey S. Murdock (Frohnmayer Deatherage Law Firm) represent defendants.

#7906. Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

The California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

But they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for quickly loading or unloading goods.

Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

Green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

Blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.

#7905. From a Life-Long Republican Contemplating the Election Results

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Yesterday's events put me in mind (as I have been on other occasions) of Kipling's The Lesson; it was discussing England's very poor performance in the Boer War (though after England ultimately won that nasty conflict), but it applies to many other contexts as well. Its opening and closing stanzas seem especially apt:

Let us admit it fairly, as a business people should, We have had no end of a lesson: it will do us no end of good.

Not on a single issue, or in one direction or twain, But conclusively, comprehensively, and several times and again ….

It was our fault, and our very great fault—and now we must turn it to use. We have forty million reasons for failure, but not a single excuse. So the more we work and the less we talk the better results we shall get— We have had an Imperial lesson; it may make us an Empire yet!

Change what needs to be changed (the lesson is political, not Imperial), and it's good advice for many situations. The question is whether enough of us will take the advice—and, of course, whether the lesson we learn is the correct one.

#7903. How To Spot a Flood-Damaged Car Before You Buy It

Learn the subtle signs to look for to avoid buying a flooded car.

With the average cost of a new car approaching $50,000, it can make more financial sense to buy used. But, while the lower price point is appealing, mechanic David Martin says to shop carefully and to check any used car for signs of flooding. “Engine computers, sensors, electrical connectors and wiring are vulnerable to corrosion, expensive to fix and could endanger lives,” he says. Not all cars that have been in a flood will be given a flood title, and unscrupulous sellers will mask this fact from would-be buyers. Ahead, learn how to tell if you’re buying a flood-damaged car, with expert-backed advice from Martin.

Use your nose to detect water damage inside the vehicle. “If the car smells musty or moldy, watch out,” Martin says. “Also, pay attention to cars that have strong air freshener or detergent scents. They could be used to mask flood-related mildew.” Additionally, look for silt or mud in glove compartments or under seats where it may have been overlooked during cleaning. Finding it is a tell-tale sign the car has been flooded. Also look carefully for condensation behind instrument panels and interior and exterior lights.

Check for any rust or flaking metal on the car’s underside, especially on brake lines and around the fuel tank, Martin says. Lift the hood and look for corrosion on the battery terminals and engine components, then open the car doors and inspect the door hinges for signs of rust.

Vehicle upholstery and carpeting can reveal signs of flooding. Feel for dampness and look for stains, as well as loose, wrinkled or buckled carpeting. Additionally, pull seat belts all the way out to check for stains, mildew or mud and look for mismatched or recently replaced carpeting and upholstery.

Turn on the car and do a thorough test of the car’s electrical components. Check the power windows, door locks, seat controls, and backup camera. “Make sure all lights, the air conditioner, heater, wipers, turn signals, stereo and navigation systems work,” Martin says. “And test them more than once.” Even if an electrical component is working, check to make sure it’s working properly. Flickering lights and intermittent functioning can also be signs of water damage.

Flood-damaged cars may be moved across state lines and retitled, so always get a Carfax report, which tracks a vehicle’s complete history regardless of location. Additionally, run the vehicle’s VIN number through the National Insurance Crime Bureau. “The service can identify whether a car has been reported stolen or labeled as salvage by insurance companies due to flooding,” Martin says. “But, while these reports can be helpful, they don’t cover everything.That’s why having a certified mechanic inspect a used car before you buy is a smart investment.”

Even if you don’t suspect a car has been flooded after looking it over yourself, a professional mechanic could catch subtle signs you missed, as well as any other mechanical issues with the vehicle. Ask them to specifically check for signs of flooding.

Yes, a flood-damaged car can still have a clean title and show no record of flooding in its history.

No, not if you intend to drive it. Issues can continue to arise years after a flooding event that can impact the vehicle’s functioning. However, you could buy a flooded car with the intention of using it for parts.

#7902. Wise Words from Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas as to Access to Court Records

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

My Stanford law school colleagues Nora and David Engstrom, as well as Berkeley law professor Jonah Gelbach and others, have asked the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules recommend a new Rule of Civil Procedure (5.3) governing the sealing of court records. I think this is an excellent idea: While there is a good deal of precedent on the question, distilling it into a rule that can easily be consulted by judges, lawyers, law clerks, and pro se litigants would be very helpful.

Just today, Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas (also a former law professor), submitted a letter endorsing the proposed rule, and I thought it was much worth passing along:

Dear Members of the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules:

I write to express my strong support for proposed Rule 5.3, a much-needed recapitulation of the procedural standards governing sealing of judicial records.

The public has a presumptive right to access judicial records. This right serves several important societal functions. By exposing the records of private wrongdoing to the public eye, this right deters further wrongdoing. By forcing the government to litigate out in the open, it empowers the public "to keep a watchful eye on the workings of public agencies." Nixon v. Warner Commc'ns, Inc., 435 U.S. 589, 598 (1978). And by enabling the public to dig into the bases for judicial decisions, it enables the public to assure itself of the strength of judicial reasoning, the cornerstone of judicial legitimacy. This right thus not only "diminishes possibilities for injustice, incompetence, perjury, and fraud," but also provides "the public with a more complete understanding of the judicial system and a better perception of its fairness." In re Avandia Mktg., Sales Prac. & Prod. Liab. Litig., 924 F.3d 662, 672 (3d Cir. 2019) (internal quotation marks omitted).

On paper, this right looks strong. In the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, where I sit, a district court issuing an order to seal "must articulate the compelling, countervailing interests to be protected" and "make specific findings on the record concerning the effects of disclosure." Id. (internal quotation marks omitted). But that standard is a paper tiger—mighty in appearance, but toothless in practice. Time and again, we see cases on appeal where the parties asked to seal large parts of the record below, and the district court, with little discussion, agreed to do so.

Take one recent motion to seal in a Third Circuit case. The district court had certified a multi-state class action against a car company. On appeal, the company asked us to seal ten volumes of appendices, totaling nearly three thousand pages of material. The company told us that sealing was necessary to prevent competitors from copying its design choices, stealing its engineering solutions, and exploiting its sales strategy.

But it took only a cursory glance at the appendices to see how overbroad the company's request was. Hundreds of pages, for example, covered deposition testimony from one of the plaintiff's lay witnesses, a mechanic who had worked on the defendant's cars and had commented on their alleged defects. Hundreds of other pages dealt with one of the plaintiffs' experts, who had opined on the veracity of the defendant's public comments and sales catalogues. But if the mechanic based his testimony on his day-to-day work on the defendant's cars, and the expert had based his testimony on the company's public statements, how would these materials reveal competitive secrets? So I denied the request without prejudice, asking the company to come back with a narrower request if it so chose. But why had the record below been sealed in the first place?

It should come as little surprise that motions to seal almost always go unopposed. The harm of overbroad sealing falls on future victims of repeat tortfeasors, future litigants in related cases, and the public at large. It does not fall on the parties to the case.

Indeed, the parties generally have an active interest in secrecy. The party who moves to seal records fears that the information produced in the case could lead to bad press coverage, competitive harms, or even follow-on litigation. The other party presumably does not share those same concerns about broad disclosure, but it does not share the public's concerns about overbroad sealing, either.

So in the give-and-take game of litigation, where it can be important to reserve your capital for fighting the fights that matter to your client, opposing a motion to seal is a waste of that capital. At the very least, it is a waste of time and money. For lawyers in an active dispute—so used to viewing themselves as only agents of their clients, and not also officers of the court—submitting an opposition to an overbroad motion to seal might not seem worth the cost of the paper to print it.

This leaves it to district-court judges to police these motions and protect the public's presumptive right of access to judicial records. But what my experience as a judge on the court of appeals has taught me, Professor Engstrom et. al's empirical work now confirms: Most district courts rubber-stamp these requests.

This might come as a surprise to some members of the Judicial Conference. After all, the law of every circuit requires district courts to reject requests to seal that are too broad to be justified by their supposed rationale.

So why do district courts frequently fail to apply that law? One problem might be the lack of developed precedent in this area. Because motions to seal are almost never subject to full treatment in district court opinions, let alone appellate review, there are few decisions applying legal standards to specific facts, teasing out what interests suffice to justify sealing, and how broad is too broad. Without clearly factually analogous precedent to rely on, district courts might be more hesitant to deny a motion to seal as overbroad, even though the operative legal standard compels that result.

Another problem is rooted in the lack of adversarial presentation. With no one on the other side, inflated claims of confidentiality go unchallenged.

Other problems might boil down to the mechanics of busy district court dockets. Perhaps, for example, when a district court grants a protective order, that decision generates an inertial force that skews the outcome of the subsequent motion to seal, even though the two decisions are subject to different legal standards. Or perhaps a motion to seal, because it is unopposed, slips under the radar, resembling an administrative matter to be rubber-stamped rather than a legal decision to be carefully scrutinized.

But whatever the reason, the results are clear: For most motions to seal, "the parties agree, the busy district court accommodates, and nobody is left in the courtroom to question whether the decision satisfied the substantive requirements." Binh Hoa Le v. Exeter Fin. Corp., 990 F.3d 410, 417 (5th Cir. 2021).

This proposed rule will push parties and courts alike to do better. First, this proposed rule will ensure that the parties know what their obligations are when they submit a motion to seal. I often sit by designation on the District of Delaware, where I regularly receive motions to seal with no accompanying explanation or justification, putting the onus on me to push the parties for more. Under Proposed Rule 5.3(c), parties will be reminded that, as our circuit has regularly held, "[b]road allegations of harm, bereft of specific examples or articulated reasoning, are insufficient." In re Avandia Mktg., 924 F.3d at 673 (internal quotation marks omitted).

Second, this proposed rule will act as a process-forcing mechanism for busy district court judges. District courts lack the benefit of adversarial litigation over motions to seal. And without a party opposing a motion, it is easy to think that no reasoning is needed for an order—if no party loses, the thinking goes, no party needs a basis for the court's decision.

Proposed Rule 5.3(h) makes clear that even without an adversarial party, the district court must act as the steward of the public interest in accessing court records, and must reason through its decision. The decision to seal is for the court to make by applying the correct legal standard, not for the parties to make by means of consent. Proposed Rule 5.3(i) provides a checklist that a district court can use in reaching that decision.

Finally, the proposed rule will remind parties and district courts alike that sealing is not an all-or-nothing question. Proposed Rule 5.3(d)(3) and (g) make clear that, where viable, the default approach should be targeted redactions. The choice is not between disclosing a list of social security numbers and sealing an entire document. A happy medium is often readily available.

This proposed rule does not make new law. Sunlight is the best disinfectant for many societal ills, yet sealing "insulates the participants" in the legal process, "masking impropriety, obscuring incompetence, and concealing corruption." Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. v. F.T.C., 710 F.2d 1165, 1179 (6th Cir. 1983). Judicial reasoning is the basis for judicial legitimacy, yet sealing "withdraws an element of the judicial process from public view," making "the ensuing decision look more like fiat." Matter of Krynicki, 983 F.2d 74, 75 (7th Cir. 1992) (Easterbrook, J.). For these reasons, the courts of appeals have consistently held that the public has a presumptive right to access judicial records, one that should only be abrogated where necessary, and even there only to the extent necessary. This proposed rule simply makes that right harder to neglect.

My then-student Jennifer Welson and I had unsuccessfully proposed a sealing rule to the Rule Committee in 2020, on behalf of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and Electronic Frontier Foundation; but I much hope that the Engstrom et al. proposal, which is backed by considerably more empirical research than mine had been, will be more successful.

#7901. If You See Cyan Lights on a Car, Here’s What They Mean

Cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars. Here's what the unusual color means and why federal regulators want to standardize it.

Colored lights play an important part in driving safety. Red brake lights mean a vehicle is slowing down, amber turn signals indicate someone is turning, flashing red and blue indicate an emergency, and yellow lights can mean a hazard or warning.

But what about cyan? Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed new federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.

Learn what the color would mean, where it’s already appearing, and what drivers should expect in the future.

Cyan lights would indicate that a vehicle’s automated driving system is in control and no one inside needs to actively monitor the road. The lights could appear on cars with someone behind the wheel or vehicles that operate without a human driver.

On Oct. 23, NHTSA announced a proposal to establish federal standards for these lights, including their placement and brightness. The lights would remain steady rather than flash, and drivers would be able to see them from all sides of the vehicle. The proposal is part of a broader effort to update safety requirements for automated vehicles, including those NHTSA describes as “vehicles designed never to be driven by a human being.”

“As automotive technology continues to evolve, our safety standards must keep pace with innovation in ways that do not compromise public safety,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in the agency’s release. “These proposed updates address unnecessary regulatory burdens for vehicles built without traditional manual controls while establishing clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps. By aligning our regulations with today’s technology, we are paving the way for safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”

Cyan would help other drivers, pedestrians, and law enforcement recognize when an automated system is handling the driving. Unlike common driver-assistance features that help with steering or speed, these systems can operate without constant human supervision under certain conditions.

The lights wouldn’t give self-driving cars any special privileges or change how other drivers should behave around them.

Mercedes-Benz has already received permission to use turquoise-colored lights on certain vehicles in California and Nevada. California approved testing on freeways, while Nevada allowed the lights on certain production vehicles.

The lights work with Mercedes-Benz’s Drive Pilot system, which can handle driving under specific conditions. A driver still needs to remain available to take control when requested. The company has tested the lights near the outside mirrors and on the front and rear of its vehicles.

“Mercedes-Benz is committed to standardizing the color turquoise,” the company said in a release, explaining that the goal is to make automated driving systems easier for people to recognize around the world.

Those approvals came before NHTSA’s latest proposal, which could establish a consistent standard for other manufacturers across the country. For now, the new federal rules are still under consideration. Even if NHTSA finalizes them, carmakers wouldn’t have to install cyan lights on self-driving vehicles. Manufacturers that choose to use them would need to follow the new standards.

Under the proposal, the lights could turn on when the automated system is driving without someone monitoring the road. They’d have to turn off when a person is expected to resume that responsibility. Drivers wouldn’t need to do anything differently when they see cyan lights, but they’d have a clearer idea of who’s controlling the vehicle.

#7900. Wolverine Loader II Review: No Break-In, No Blisters

Published Nov 6, 2026 1:24 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

New work boots can be miserable until they’re broken in, especially if you spend long days on your feet. My husband, a contractor who also works on our farm, tested the Wolverine Loader II HyperRest CarbonMAX boots for a full week, wearing them up to 10 hours a day. We had previously tested two of Wolverine’s Infinity System work boots, so we were curious to compare them with this pair’s comfort design. Here’s what we found. (And for more options, see our team-tested best work boots guide.)

The break-in was the biggest surprise of our test. My husband put the Wolverine Loader II boots on and went straight to work. There was no period of stiff leather rubbing against his ankles, no uncomfortable pressure around his toes, and no need to alternate with an older pair while the new boots softened up.

He wore them for a week while doing his regular contracting work and handling chores on our farm, including clearing trees and operating equipment. Some days stretched to 10 hours, but he never complained about sore feet afterward.

Wolverine credits much of that comfort to its (removable) HyperRest footbed, which cushions and supports the foot, and a polyurethane midsole that helps absorb the impact of walking on hard surfaces. The padded collar also helps prevent rubbing around the ankle. Whatever the combination, it worked well for him from the first day.

In our testing, yes. My husband is accustomed to wearing work boots, so he knows the difference between a pair that feels good in the store and one that remains comfortable through a full shift.

The Loader II passed that test. He especially liked how light they felt for boots with protective toes. Wolverine lists the weight at 2.04 pounds per boot, and the CarbonMAX composite toe provides impact and compression protection without the bulk of a traditional steel toe.

The rubber wedge outsole is another feature of the comfort design. Its broad contact area helps distribute weight on hard, flat surfaces, which can be particularly helpful for contractors who spend hours on concrete or other unforgiving flooring.

The Wolverine Loader II is more than just a comfortable boot. Its CarbonMAX toe meets ASTM F2413-24 impact and compression requirements, and the boot also carries electrical hazard and slip-resistance ratings.

The waterproof full-grain leather upper includes reinforced toe and heel bumpers, which help protect areas that often take a beating around tools, equipment, and construction materials. A breathable waterproof membrane and moisture-wicking lining provide additional protection in wet conditions.

Wolverine also uses Goodyear welt construction, which allows the boots to be resoled rather than discarded when the outsole wears out. That’s a welcome feature in a work boot intended for regular use.

One consideration is the wedge outsole. While it’s designed for dependable traction, its relatively flat profile didn’t dig into deep mud as aggressively as some heavily lugged soles. For workers who spend most of their time in muddy fields or on steep, loose terrain, outsole design deserves extra attention.

At $169.95, the Loader II is cheaper than the premium Wolverine Infinity System boots we previously tested, yet it delivered the comfort my husband needs for long workdays.

I think these boots are particularly well suited to contractors, carpenters, equipment operators, and other tradespeople who want safety-toe protection without stiff, heavy footwear. The 6-inch lace-up design also provides a more adjustable fit than a pull-on boot.

After a week of demanding use, my husband had no complaints about comfort, fit, or foot fatigue. That’s an excellent start, although we’ll need more time to judge how the leather, stitching, and outsole hold up over months of daily wear.

For workers who dread breaking in a new pair of boots, the Loader II might just be the ticket.

#7899. Fifth Circuit on Pseudonymity of Libel Defendant (Who Claims She Was Sexually Assaulted)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Doe v. Roe, decided today by Fifth Circuit Judges Jennifer Walker Elrod, Carolyn Dineen King, and Carl Stewart:

After receiving notice of Jane Roe's impending California lawsuit involving allegations of sexual assault and sexual harassment, John Doe sued Roe in the Southern District of Mississippi, alleging that Roe was attempting to extort and defame him. Roe moved to proceed pseudonymously in the Mississippi lawsuit. The district court denied her permission to do so. Roe appeals that decision, raising several concerns with the district court's analysis. Because we agree with some of Roe's arguments, we vacate and remand for the district court to reconsider whether Roe should be allowed to proceed pseudonymously….

Roe argues that allegations of sexual assault involve matters of the utmost intimacy [and can thus justify pseudonymity]. We agree. There is no doubt that requiring alleged rape and sexual assault victims to proceed "under their real identities would require them to disclose information of the utmost intimacy." It is no surprise, then, that numerous courts have allowed alleged victims of sexual misconduct to proceed under a pseudonym, "including when they are defendants being sued for libel and related torts."

We agree with Roe. To start, we are not persuaded that the proverbial cat is out of the bag here. True, publicly available information cannot be obscured by courts. However, that internet sleuths might speculate that Roe is a particular person because her California complaint "lines up with [her] public profile" is not the same as a public broadcasting of Roe's certain identity. As to the fact that Roe's name was a matter of public record for short periods, that was either because of Doe's actions (which Roe objected to), or Roe's inadvertent disclosures which counsel corrected and constituted no waiver (which we address below)….

Last, Roe argues that she did not waive her right to proceed anonymously. Again, we agree. Roe never waived her ability to request pseudonymity because her conduct does not constitute an "intentional relinquishment" of that position. Roe's opposition to Doe's motion to proceed pseudonymously waived nothing because Roe's position was that she should be allowed to proceed pseudonymously while he should not be. And any confusion about Roe's position based on the precise language in her opposition brief was clarified by her own subsequent motions seeking to seal or redact Doe's amended complaint (which used Roe's real name) and to proceed pseudonymously.

Further, Doe's use of Roe's real name in open court did not constitute waiver on Roe's behalf because, at the time, Doe had already publicly named Roe in his amended complaint, Roe had a pending motion seeking to seal or redact that amended complaint naming her, and Roe objected to the use of her name at the hearing (even if not as fast as a prudent attorney likely should have). Finally, we are not convinced that Roe's inadvertent disclosures of her real name in the California case and on this appeal constitute waiver. The disclosures were unintentional, were made in portions of larger filings, and Roe took steps to correct the errors once becoming aware of them, resulting in the sealing and refiling of the documents. These facts do not demonstrate that Roe intentionally relinquished her request to proceed pseudonymously….

In light of the clarifications provided in this opinion, we find that it is appropriate to allow the district court to reconsider whether Roe should be permitted to proceed under a pseudonym in this case. {We acknowledge Doe's argument that allowing Roe to proceed under a pseudonym would be prejudicial to him. We think that argument is best left for the district court to address in the first instance on remand.}

NEXT: Wise Words from Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas as to Access to Court Records

Over-the-top outdoor holiday decorations make the whole neighborhood get in the festive spirit! To help inspire you, we found some of the best maximalist holiday homes from coast to coast.

#7896. 16 Types of Blinds Every Homeowner Should Know

Updated Nov 6, 2026 1:46 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you’ve weighed the benefits of curtains, shutters, and blinds in your search for the right window coverings for your home and you’ve settled on blinds, you’re in good company. According to a study by research firm Market Research Future, the size of the window blind market was an estimated $75.48 billion in 2025, and it’s expected to grow to $136.35 billion by 2035. Another research firm, Global Market Insights, found that blinds and shades dominated the window treatment industry in 2025.

With so many different types of blinds on the market, how do you decide which will suit your home best? Whether you’re looking for something sleek and modern or traditional and classic, this guide will help you figure out which ones might be the right pick for your windows.

Blinds are a type of window covering composed of numerous slats, vertical or horizontal, that can be tilted or rotated to adjust the amount of light entering a space. Blinds made of aluminum or vinyl are typically the most cost-efficient types, but there also are blinds crafted of fabric and wood.

They can be installed inside the window frame or above it. Window blinds are typically mounted with specially designed brackets that are sold with the blinds.

The slats are suspended from a track that runs along the top of a window frame. This style of blinds collects less dust than other types of blinds and is easy to clean. The slats just need to be wiped down with a damp cloth.

Best For: Affordability and minimal maintenance

Blinds.com’s vertical blinds are textured, available in a variety of colors, and are guaranteed to fit.

The Home Decorators faux wood Venetian blinds are cordless, making them safe for households with pets or young children.

Mini blinds are like Venetian blinds, with some minor differences. Like Venetian blinds, they are typically made from aluminum or vinyl instead of wood or bamboo. Mini blinds’ slats, however, are usually an inch wide or narrower. While these two types of blinds perform the same way, mini blinds have a sleeker design and thus tend to look more modern and contemporary.

With a minimalist design and cordless operation, the Achim mini blinds are safe and stylish.

Because vinyl blinds are made from PVC and other synthetic materials, they’re a great choice for bathrooms, kitchens, and other areas prone to moisture and humidity. They’re very easy to clean with a cloth or a vacuum attachment. If you’re looking for a window treatment that helps insulate your windows or provides soundproofing, vinyl isn’t your best bet. Still, they are a lot cheaper than wood and other options, if you’re on a budget.

Best For: Budget-conscious shoppers; moisture-prone rooms

Ideal for high-humidity spaces like garages and bathrooms, Bali’s 2-inch vinyl blinds resist chipping and warping and come in dozens of colors.

Wood blinds are a popular choice for those looking to add an element of luxury to their window treatments since wood blinds offer a natural, timeless look that never goes out of style. Not only do they exude sophistication, but they are also incredibly durable and can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. They can be painted or stained to match any color palette, and different slat sizes are available to accommodate shoppers’ specific needs. Wooden blinds tend to be horizontal—or Venetian—style, though vertical wooden blinds are also available.

Best For: Homeowners who are in it for the long haul—these are built to last

Levolor’s 2-inch wood blinds have cordless lift and wand tilt and come in a variety of wood stains.

Sometimes you want the timeless look of a wood blind but don’t have the budget for it. Enter the faux wood blind, which is usually made from PVC or a wood/synthetic blend. Faux wood blinds look like the real deal (though your mileage may vary when it comes to how authentic the wood grain looks), at a fraction of the price. The best part? They can be installed in high-humidity spaces like laundry rooms and bathrooms, where natural wood blinds would mold and warp.

Best for: Budget-conscious homeowners who want a timeless look

Blinds.com’s faux wood blinds are moisture resistant, and available in a variety of wood stains and painted colors.

Aluminum blinds are one of the most popular types of window blinds because of their affordable price and lightweight yet durable design. A sleek, modern look that can complement many decor styles, they are easy to install and incredibly long-lasting. Aluminum blinds also come in a variety of colors, sizes, and textures, allowing homeowners to customize the look of their windows to suit many different aesthetics. In terms of energy efficiency, aluminum blinds help keep a home’s interior cooler by reflecting the sun’s rays away from the window. This helps reduce air conditioning costs since less energy is required to maintain steady temperatures inside the house.

Best For: Easy installation and durability

Sleek and affordable, Blinds.com’s 8-gauge aluminum blinds are available in a variety of neutral colors.

If you’re looking for blinds to cover sliding doors or large windows, consider panel blinds. These window treatments are composed of several panels affixed to a headrail at the top of the window. Each panel is attached to a carrier that slides along a track in order to open or close the blinds. They offer a unique look that differs from standard vertical blinds, making them a great choice for design-forward shoppers.

Roller blinds are technically a type of window shade. An alternative to curtains, these shades are made up of a single piece of fabric material that rolls up and down to control the amount of sunlight that enters the space. Roller shades can be made from a variety of fabrics, ranging from sheer materials to opaque options. While roller blinds might have a reputation for being low quality and not performing well, their design has actually come a long way in recent years.

Chicology’s blackout roller shade has a cordless design and is made from hypoallergenic polyester that won’t attract dust.

UNISHASDES bamboo blinds  partially filter sunlight and come in a variety of sizes and finishes.

Motorized blinds are modern window coverings that you can open and close using a remote control, phone app, or via voice command. Some models have light sensors that automate the opening and closing of your blinds at certain times of the day. Unlike traditional blinds that are adjusted manually, motorized blinds have electric or battery-powered motors that raise and lower them. If you want to be able to control the lighting in a room without ever having to leave your seat, opt for blinds with this feature.

Custom Home Collection’s wood blinds come in over 100 colors and a motorized lift option, which is ideal for smart homes and hard-to-reach windows.

Coolaroo’s knitted HDPE roller shades are mold resistant and block 90 percent of UV rays. Read the review.

Our Recommendation: Coolaroo Exterior Roller Shade at Amazon, priced from $35.25.This exterior window treatment is affordable, cordless, protects against UV rays, and comes in a wide range of finishes.

Sometimes called layered or dual shades, zebra blinds consist of two layers of fabric, each with alternating horizontal bands of sheer and opaque fabric. You can adjust, or roll, the fabric to line up the stripes on the two layers of fabric, meaning opaque is lined up with opaque, and sheer with sheer; this allows light to enter. If you roll the shade such that the opaque stripes on one layer are lined up with the sheer strips on the other layer, the effect is that of an opaque shade, and no light comes through.

Chicology’s zebra blinds are cordless (and thus kid-friendly), light-filtering, and come in three colors.

Also called cellular blinds or cellular shades, honeycomb blinds are constructed of two sheets of fabric that are seamed together horizontally at regular intervals. When looking at these blinds from the side, the resulting pattern somewhat resembles that of a honeycomb. Highly insulating, the design is considered one of the most energy-efficient, and the cellular construction is also good at noise cancellation

Best For: Energy efficiency; homes with a modern vibe

Noise-dampening, cordless, and energy-efficient, the BlindsAvenue honeycomb blinds can be mounted inside or outside the window.

Pleated blinds are made from a single length of woven fabric that is pressed into sharp, horizontal pleats at regular intervals, yielding a zig-zag appearance. The blind is raised or lowered to adjust the amount of light entering the room. While they’re often compared to honeycomb blinds, pleated blinds don’t offer the same insulating properties as cellular blinds. Pleated blinds offer a clean, modern look.

Best For: Decorators in search of an elegant, minimalist look.

Semi-sheer and cordless, these pull-down blinds from Calyx Interiors are available in four colors and several sizes.

Best For: Rooms in which someone needs to sleep during the day.

These cordless, pull-down blackout blinds from Persilux are available in five colors and multiple sizes.

Our Recommendation: Persilux Custom, Cordless Blackout Cellular Blinds at Amazon starting at $63.99. These cordless, pull-down blinds are available in five colors and numerous sizes.

#7895. That Hole in Your Ruler Isn’t Random – Here’s What It’s Actually For

That small hole on a ruler has a practical purpose and an unexpected history. Here's why it exists and how people use it.

Almost everyone has used a ruler at some point, whether it was for a school project, measuring something around the house, or drawing a straight line. But even after years of using one, there’s a small detail that’s easy to miss: the hole near the end.

Those holes in rulers aren’t just part of the design. They actually serve a purpose, and the reason they’re there goes back further than most people might expect. Here’s what they’re for, how they were used in the past, and a few other ways they come in handy.

The hole at the end of a ruler is mainly there for storage. It lets people hang the ruler on a hook, nail, or pegboard instead of leaving it in a drawer or on a workbench. This is particularly helpful with longer metal rulers that might not fit in a toolbox.

But the hole has been around for much longer than modern workshops. Years ago, before paper notebooks became common in schools, students practiced writing on small slate boards. They could wipe away their writing with a damp cloth and use the board again.

Some students tied that cloth to their rulers with a piece of string through the hole. That way, they always had something nearby to clean their slates. Schools eventually moved away from slate boards, but the holes remained. Today, they’re mostly there to make rulers easier to hang and store.

Hanging a ruler isn’t the only reason manufacturers add holes. Some rulers have several, and they can serve different purposes depending on where they’re placed. For example, certain school rulers have three holes spaced along one side. These line up with the rings in a standard three-ring binder, so students can keep their rulers with their other school supplies.

Some rulers also have holes that help with drawing circles. A pin through one hole can hold the ruler in place while a pencil in another hole traces a circle as the ruler turns. Not every ruler has holes designed for this, but specialty models like the Creative Grids Quick Trim Ruler do. A compass is still a better choice when exact measurements matter.

Some crafting rulers have holes for more specific jobs. Quilting rulers and templates may have openings that help mark circles or line up fabric before cutting. Others have slots or shaped edges that guide a rotary cutter, making it easier to cut certain shapes.

There are also special rulers for paper crafts and stitching. Some have rows of tiny, evenly spaced holes that help people mark where to make stitches or decorative patterns.

Of course, not every ruler has holes. Smaller plastic rulers often don’t need them, while longer metal versions may have one at each end. It mostly comes down to how the manufacturer expects people to use the ruler. And for everyday measuring, the holes don’t make much difference. A ruler without them can measure just as accurately as one with them.
